There is no TTL, no polling, no revalidation on `visibilitychange`/`focus`, and no realtime subscription to Supabase.

This is a shared leaderboard: several people log games from their own devices against the same `leaderboards` row. A tab left open shows stale standings indefinitely — every render path (`spotlightHTML`, `sportTablesHTML`, `padelTableHTML`, `padelSessionBanner`, `openGames`) reads from this snapshot.

The staleness is also time-based, not just write-based: `api.loadBoard()` resolves `localToday()` once at fetch time and filters `v_daily_losses` on `game_date=eq.<today>` (`js/api.js:179` and `js/api.js:187`). A tab open across midnight keeps rendering yesterday's row under the "Today's biggest loser" heading, while `padelSpotlightHTML` (line 1013) recomputes today's padel loser against a freshly-evaluated `api.localToday()` — so the two spotlights disagree about what "today" means.

The Americano round-runner is the worst case: `openSessionRunner` can stay open for a whole padel night while another phone logs rounds into the same `session_id`, and the live "tonight" standings silently omit them.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, add an invalidation strategy for the module-level `data` cache. At minimum: (1) record the fetch time alongside `data` in `loadBoard()`, and re-run `refresh()` on `document.visibilitychange` / `window.focus` when the snapshot is older than a short TTL (e.g. 30–60s); (2) also invalidate when `api.localToday()` no longer matches the date captured at fetch time, so the "Today's biggest loser" spotlight and `dailyLosses` do not survive a midnight rollover; (3) for `openSessionRunner`, poll `refresh()` + `draw()` on an interval (or subscribe to Supabase realtime on `sports_games`) while the runner sheet is open, clearing the interval in the sheet's close handler.

violations.title: `rosterMem` grows without bound and is never cleared when its board or players are removed
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a plain object cache keyed `${boardId}:${sport}` holding the last A/B roster split, written in `openLogSport`'s save handler (line 532) and read by `restore()` (lines 429–434). Nothing ever deletes an entry: not `openDeleteBoard` (which deletes the board and all its players), not `deletePlayer`/`restorePlayer`, not `switchBoard`.

`restore()` does filter out ids missing from `activePlayers()`, which prevents deleted players leaking into the picker, so the user-visible impact is limited. What remains is an entry-per-board-per-sport that accumulates for the lifetime of the page — including entries keyed to boards that no longer exist — and a subtle behavioural quirk: a player archived and later restored silently reappears pre-selected in the roster from a session logged before they were archived.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, invalidate `rosterMem` entries when their source data disappears: delete all keys starting with `${boardId}:` inside `openDeleteBoard`'s success branch, and drop the cached ids for a player in the `deletePlayer` handler in `openPlayers`. Alternatively store the roster memory with a timestamp and treat entries older than the current session (or older than a few hours) as expired inside `restore()`.
violations.snippet:
let lastSport = 'tt_singles';
const rosterMem = {};   // `${boardId}:${sport}` -> { a:[ids], b:[ids] }

violations.title: Lockout counter in `fails` is never invalidated when its window expires
violations.content:
The in-memory `fails` map stores `{ n, until }` per IP, but the failure count `n` is only ever cleared on a *successful* passcode (`fails.delete(ip)` on line 128). When the lockout window at line 116 (`rec.until > now`) elapses, the stale `n` value survives — nothing resets it. On the next wrong passcode, line 123 computes `n = (rec?.n ?? 0) + 1`, which is already `>= MAX_FAILS`, so line 124 immediately re-locks the IP for another `LOCK_MS`.

The practical effect: once an IP crosses 5 failures, a single mistyped passcode at any later point — hours or days later — triggers a fresh 60s lockout, because the counter is stale cached state that never expires alongside the `until` timestamp it is paired with. The intended "5 wrong passcodes -> 60s cooldown" behaviour silently degrades into "1 wrong passcode -> 60s cooldown, forever" for that IP. For a shared-NAT friend group all hitting the same egress IP, one person's typo locks out everyone.

The fix is to treat an expired `until` as an invalidation signal and restart the count from zero.

violations.title: `fails` map has no eviction, so expired entries accumulate unboundedly
violations.content:
`const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>()` retains an entry per distinct client IP for the lifetime of the function instance. Entries are removed only on a successful passcode (line 128); an IP that fails once and never returns leaves its record in the map permanently. The `until` field encodes an expiry for the *lockout*, but nothing ever sweeps entries whose `until` has passed.

Each record is small, so this is not an immediate risk for a friend-group app on a warm instance, but the map is fed directly from the attacker-controlled `x-forwarded-for` header (line 113). A stream of requests with varied `X-Forwarded-For` values inserts an unbounded number of never-collected keys, and the retained stale entries are also what make the counter bug above persist indefinitely. A periodic or opportunistic sweep of records whose `until` has elapsed bounds the memory and gives the cached state a real expiry.
violations.snippet: const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>();

violations.title: Admin passcode stored verbatim in `sessionStorage` by `unlock`
violations.content:
`unlock` writes the raw admin passcode into `sessionStorage` under `KEY`. `sessionStorage` is fully readable by any JavaScript running on the origin, so a single XSS flaw (or a malicious/compromised third-party script, browser extension, or injected inline handler) can read the plaintext credential and replay it against the API for as long as it stays valid. Because this is the shared secret itself rather than a derived, scoped, short-lived token, exfiltration grants full admin capability and cannot be revoked per-session — it requires rotating the passcode for every user.

The surrounding code renders user-supplied strings via `el(\`...\`)` template HTML (see `openNewBoard` in `js/app.js`), which raises the practical likelihood of an injection sink reaching this value.

Preferred fix: have the server exchange the passcode for a session credential set as an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie so JavaScript never holds it. If the deployment cannot issue cookies, at minimum exchange the passcode for a short-lived, server-issued bearer token, keep it in a module-scoped in-memory variable instead of `sessionStorage`, and never persist the passcode itself.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, remove the plaintext passcode persistence in `unlock` (line 199). Replace it with a server-side exchange: POST the passcode to an auth endpoint that validates it and sets a short-lived `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` session cookie, then have the API layer rely on the cookie (`credentials: 'include'`) instead of reading `sessionStorage`. Update any callers that read `KEY` from `sessionStorage` accordingly, and drop the `KEY` storage constant if it becomes unused. If an `HttpOnly` cookie is not possible in this deployment, at minimum store only a short-lived server-issued token in a module-scoped in-memory variable (cleared on reload) rather than persisting the passcode to `sessionStorage`.
violations.snippet: export const unlock = (passcode) => { sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, passcode); };

violations.title: Admin passcode hardcoded in client-side JavaScript as `LOSER_WORD`
violations.content:
`LOSER_WORD` is a hardcoded shared secret (`'pecundang'`) shipped in browser JavaScript, and the adjacent comment directs the operator to set the server-side `ADMIN_PASSCODE` secret to this exact word. It is passed as the `secret` argument to `api.logGame`, `api.undoLast`, `api.logSportsGame`, and `api.createPadelSession`, which forward it to `call()` in `js/api.js` as the `passcode` field the admin Edge Function verifies.

Because the write-authorization secret and the admin passcode are the same value, and that value is readable in the page source, the `openPasscode` unlock gate provides no protection: any visitor can read `js/app.js`, recover the passcode, and invoke privileged actions such as `delete_leaderboard`, `delete_game`, and `delete_player` directly against the Edge Function. Storing an authorization credential in client-delivered code means it cannot be rotated without a redeploy and is exposed to every user, crawler, and cache.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, decouple the confess-word from the admin passcode. Keep `LOSER_WORD` as a UI-only string used to parse which player lost, and stop passing it as the `secret` argument to `api.logGame`, `api.undoLast`, `api.logSportsGame`, and `api.createPadelSession`. On the server side, introduce a separate, low-privilege credential path for the log/undo/session-create actions distinct from `ADMIN_PASSCODE`, so that possession of the client-visible word cannot authorize destructive actions (`delete_leaderboard`, `delete_game`, `delete_player`, `rename_leaderboard`). Change the deployed `ADMIN_PASSCODE` secret to a value that is never embedded in client code, and update the comment above `LOSER_WORD` so it no longer instructs operators to reuse the confess-word as the admin passcode.

violations.title: Wildcard CORS origin fails open when `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` is unset
violations.content:
`corsHeaders` falls back to `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: '*'` whenever the `ALLOWED` list is empty (line 39), and `ALLOWED` is derived from the optional `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` env var via `?? ''` (line 17). This is a fail-open default: if `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` is never set, is cleared, or is set to a value that filters down to an empty list (e.g. only whitespace or commas), the function silently begins accepting cross-origin browser requests from **any** site — with no deploy-time error and no log line to signal the misconfiguration.

This matters more than usual here because this function is, per its own header comment, "the ONLY write path" and it runs with the `service_role` key, which bypasses RLS. The preflight also explicitly allows the `authorization` and `apikey` headers (line 32), so an arbitrary origin is permitted to send them.

The practical exploitability is limited — `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is never set, so browsers will not attach cookies, and every action is still gated behind `passcodeMatches`. So this is a defence-in-depth / deployment-safety problem rather than a direct authentication bypass. Still, the origin allowlist is the intended second layer, and a fallback that quietly disables it based on a missing env var is the wrong default for the production write path. The dev-convenience case should be opted into explicitly rather than inferred from absence of config.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the permissive CORS fallback explicit instead of inferred from a missing env var.

1. Add a dedicated dev flag, e.g. `const DEV_OPEN_CORS = Deno.env.get('DEV_OPEN_CORS') === 'true';`
2. In `corsHeaders`, only emit `h['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = '*'` when `DEV_OPEN_CORS` is true. Otherwise, set the header only when `ALLOWED.includes(origin)` — omitting it entirely for non-matching origins, as the current `else if` branch already does correctly.
3. At module load, if `ALLOWED.length === 0 && !DEV_OPEN_CORS`, emit a clear startup warning via `console.warn` (or throw) so a missing/empty `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` is loud rather than silent.

Keep the existing `Vary: Origin` header and the `authorization, apikey, content-type` allow-headers list unchanged.

violations.title: `log_sports_game` discards the `points_target` query error and silently falls back to 21
violations.content: Unlike every other query in this handler, the padel board lookup destructures only `data` and drops `error`. If the `leaderboards` select fails (connection error, RLS, timeout), `board` is `undefined` and `padelTarget` silently becomes `21`. Execution then continues as if the lookup succeeded: `scoreError(sport, score_a, score_b, 21)` validates the round against the wrong target and the game is inserted with `points_target: 21`, permanently snapshotting a value the board never configured. A board with `points_target: 32` would have rounds silently accepted/rejected against 21 and stored wrong, with no error surfaced to the caller and nothing logged.
violations.fixPrompt: In the `log_sports_game` case of `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, capture the error from the padel `points_target` lookup: `const { data: board, error: ebt } = await db.from('leaderboards').select('points_target').eq('id', leaderboard_id).maybeSingle();` then `if (ebt) return bad(ebt.message);` before defaulting `padelTarget = board?.points_target ?? 21`. Only fall back to 21 when the query succeeded and the column is null.
violations.snippet:
const { data: board } = await db.from('leaderboards').select('points_target').eq('id', leaderboard_id).maybeSingle();
          padelTarget = board?.points_target ?? 21;

violations.title: Top-level catch turns every unexpected failure into a 400 with a raw internal message
violations.content: The single `catch (e)` around the whole action switch performs no type discrimination and returns `bad(...)`, which defaults to HTTP 400. A `TypeError` from a null dereference, a Supabase client connection failure, or any other server-side fault is therefore reported to the client as a client-side validation error, sitting alongside genuine 400s like `'game_date must be YYYY-MM-DD'`. The client in `js/api.js` surfaces that raw message verbatim, so users see internal messages (and callers/monitoring cannot distinguish "your input was wrong" from "the server broke"). The blind `(e as Error)` cast also yields `undefined` for non-`Error` throws, producing `{"ok":false,"error":undefined}`.
violations.fixPrompt: In the top-level catch of `Deno.serve` in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, return a 500 with a generic client-facing message for unexpected errors (e.g. `return bad('internal error', 500)`), while logging the full detail server-side. Extract the message safely, e.g. `const msg = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e);`, instead of casting with `(e as Error)`.

violations.title: Top-level error log records only `message`, discarding the stack trace
violations.content: `log(false, { error: (e as Error).message })` is the only record of an unexpected server failure, and it keeps just the message. The stack trace, error name/type, and any `cause` chain are dropped, so a production failure logs something like `{"error":"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')"}` with no indication of which of the ~20 action branches threw it. That makes the most severe class of bug in this function the hardest one to diagnose.
violations.fixPrompt: In the top-level catch of `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, include the stack and type in the log payload, e.g. `log(false, { error: e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e), name: (e as Error)?.name, stack: (e as Error)?.stack })`, so the server log retains the full context.
violations.snippet: log(false, { error: (e as Error).message });

violations.title: `restore_player`'s 404 `'player not found'` branch is unreachable; PostgREST error is returned instead
violations.content: `.single()` makes PostgREST return an error (PGRST116, "JSON object requested, multiple (or no) rows returned") when the update matches zero rows, so `if (error) return bad(error.message)` fires first and `if (!data) return bad('player not found', 404)` is dead code. A request for a non-existent `player_id` gets a 400 with an opaque PostgREST message instead of the intended 404 `'player not found'`. `rename_leaderboard` at lines 160–162 has the identical dead 404 branch for `'leaderboard not found'`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `restore_player` (and `rename_leaderboard`) in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, use `.maybeSingle()` instead of `.single()` so a zero-row update yields `data === null` rather than an error, letting the intended `bad('player not found', 404)` / `bad('leaderboard not found', 404)` branch run. Alternatively, detect the `PGRST116` code on the error and map it to the 404 message.

violations.title: `add_player` forwards any DB error as a 400, though the comment assumes only a unique violation
violations.content: The comment ("unique(leaderboard_id,name) violation lands here") documents one expected cause, but `if (error) return bad(error.message)` funnels every failure — FK violation on a bad `leaderboard_id`, connection loss, statement timeout, permission error — through the same 400 response carrying a raw Postgres string. The user sees a duplicate-name style failure for what may be an infrastructure outage, and there is no `log(false, ...)` call on this path, so the failure is invisible in the logs too. The same undiscriminated `return bad(error.message)` pattern repeats across the switch (lines 146, 170, 202, 207, 244, 259, 271, 279, 340, 355, 369, 377, 412).
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, add a helper that maps Supabase/PostgREST errors to responses by `error.code` — e.g. `23505` (unique violation) → 400 with a friendly "a player with that name already exists", `23503` (FK violation) → 400 "unknown leaderboard", everything else → 500 with a generic message plus a `log(false, { code: error.code, message: error.message, details: error.details })` server-side entry. Route the `if (error)` branches through that helper instead of `bad(error.message)`.
violations.snippet:
const { data, error } = await db.from('players').insert({ leaderboard_id, name }).select().single();
        if (error) return bad(error.message); // unique(leaderboard_id,name) violation lands here

violations.title: Request body parse error is caught bare and discarded entirely
violations.content: `try { body = await req.json(); } catch { return bad('bad request'); }` binds no error variable, so the `SyntaxError` (which states exactly where the JSON is malformed) is thrown away and never logged. The caller receives only `'bad request'`, and the server keeps no record at all, making malformed-client-payload reports impossible to investigate.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, change the body parse to `catch (e) { console.log(JSON.stringify({ at: 'admin', ip, ok: false, error: 'bad json', detail: e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e) })); return bad('request body must be valid JSON'); }` so the parse detail is retained server-side.
violations.snippet: try { body = await req.json(); } catch { return bad('bad request'); }

violations.title: `call` swallows the JSON parse failure and reports a misleading `Request failed (200)`
violations.content: `res.json().catch(() => ({}))` discards the parse error and substitutes `{}`. For a successful HTTP response with an unparseable or empty body (proxy-truncated response, HTML error page from an edge failure, 204), `out.ok` is `undefined`, so line 213 throws `Request failed (200)` — an error message that contradicts itself and describes a failure mode that did not occur. The real cause (the body was not JSON) is completely lost, and the same message is produced for network-level and body-level problems alike.
violations.fixPrompt: In `call` in `js/api.js`, capture the parse failure distinctly, e.g. `let out; try { out = await res.json(); } catch (e) { throw new Error(res.ok ? `Server sent an unreadable response (${res.status})` : `Request failed (${res.status})`, { cause: e }); }` and only then check `!res.ok || !out.ok`.
violations.snippet:
const out = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
  if (!res.ok || !out.ok) throw new Error(out.error || `Request failed (${res.status})`);

violations.title: `attempt` decides to lock the session by regex-matching the error message text
violations.content: `attempt` catches everything with no discrimination and then infers auth failure from `/passcode/i.test(e.message)`. This couples control flow to server-side prose: the server also returns messages that merely mention the passcode without being auth failures, and any future rewording of `'wrong passcode'` (index.ts:126) silently breaks the lock behaviour, leaving the user with a stale session. Conversely, an unrelated error whose text happens to contain "passcode" logs the user out. The catch also reads `e.message` unguarded, so a non-`Error` throw sets the error element to `undefined` and skips the lock. Every other failure is written to the DOM and swallowed with no logging, so unexpected client bugs leave no trace in the console.
violations.fixPrompt: Make the auth failure explicit instead of text-matched: in `js/api.js`, attach a status/code to the thrown error (e.g. `const err = new Error(out.error || `Request failed (${res.status})`); err.status = res.status; throw err;`), then in `attempt` in `js/app.js` branch on `e.status === 401` rather than `/passcode/i.test(e.message)`. Also guard the message extraction (`e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`) and `console.error(e)` before swallowing so the stack reaches the console.

violations.title: `refresh` and `switchBoard` reduce every failure to `e.message`, dropping stack and type
violations.content: Both `refresh` (lines 135–136) and `switchBoard` (line 142) catch broadly and keep only `e.message` in the `error` state variable, with no `console.error(e)`. The stack trace, error type, and any `cause` chain set upstream are discarded, so a `TypeError` inside `loadBoards`/`loadBoard` is indistinguishable from a server-reported validation failure and leaves nothing in the console to locate it. Because `e.message` is read unguarded, a non-`Error` throw (e.g. a rejected promise with a string) sets `error = undefined`, which renders as no error at all while the UI shows stale data.
violations.fixPrompt: In `refresh` and `switchBoard` in `js/app.js`, log the raw error before reducing it for display: `catch (e) { console.error(e); error = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e); }` so the stack survives in the console and non-`Error` throws still produce a visible message.
violations.snippet:
try { await loadBoards(); await loadBoard(); error = null; }
  catch (e) { error = e.message; }

violations.title: Rate-limit counter `fails` read before two `await`s, then written — lost updates defeat lockout
violations.content:
The module-level `fails` map is the only brute-force protection on the admin passcode. The handler reads `const rec = fails.get(ip)` at line 115, then crosses two async boundaries (`await req.json()` at line 119 and `await passcodeMatches(passcode)` at line 122) before writing `fails.set(ip, { n, ... })` at line 124, where `n` is derived from the stale `rec` captured earlier.

Deno serves requests concurrently in a single isolate, so N simultaneous wrong-passcode requests from the same IP all observe the same `rec.n` and all write back the same `n = rec.n + 1`. The counter advances by one instead of N, so an attacker issuing parallel (rather than serial) guesses can make far more than `MAX_FAILS` attempts before `until` is ever set. The same interleaving lets a request that read `rec` before a successful login's `fails.delete(ip)` (line 128) re-insert a stale counter afterwards.

The check at line 116 (`rec.until > now`) is likewise a check-then-act: the lockout decision is made on a snapshot taken before the passcode comparison, so requests already in flight when the lock engages are not blocked.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `fails` counter update atomic with respect to the read. Re-read the record from `fails` immediately before mutating it (after the `await passcodeMatches(...)` call) instead of reusing the `rec` snapshot captured at line 115, e.g. `const cur = fails.get(ip); const n = (cur?.n ?? 0) + 1; fails.set(ip, { n, until: n >= MAX_FAILS ? Date.now() + LOCK_MS : 0 });`. Also re-check the lockout (`cur.until > Date.now()`) at that point so requests that were in flight when the lock engaged are rejected.

violations.title: `undo_last` selects the newest game then deletes it in a separate query
violations.content:
`undo_last` reads the newest game id with one query (lines 251-255) and deletes it with a second query (line 258). Two concurrent undo requests for the same `leaderboard_id` both read the same `last.id`, then both issue the delete. The first removes the row; the second deletes zero rows but still returns `ok(last)` and logs success, so the user is told two games were undone when only one was. Conversely, a `log_game` that commits between the select and the delete causes the undo to remove the second-newest game rather than the one the user just logged.

The undo button is reachable from the "pecundang" overlay (`js/app.js:393-395`) which can be double-tapped, making the concurrent path reachable in normal use.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make `undo_last` atomic: perform the delete and read the affected row in one statement, e.g. a Postgres RPC (`delete from games where id = (select id from games where leaderboard_id = $1 order by created_at desc, id desc limit 1) returning id`) called via `db.rpc(...)`. If keeping two queries, add `.select()` to the delete and return `ok(null)` when no row was actually removed so a duplicate undo does not report false success.

violations.title: `undo_last_sports` selects the newest racquet game then deletes it non-atomically
violations.content: Same check-then-act pattern as `undo_last`: the newest `sports_games` row is selected (lines 347-351) and deleted in a separate query (line 354). Concurrent undos both read the same `last.id`; the losing request deletes nothing yet returns `ok(last)` and logs success. A `log_sports_game` committing between the two queries makes the undo delete the wrong round — particularly damaging during an Americano session where rounds are logged in rapid succession from `js/app.js:720-733`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make `undo_last_sports` atomic by moving the select+delete into a single Postgres RPC with `delete ... where id = (select ... limit 1) returning id`, or at minimum add `.select()` to the delete and return `ok(null)` when zero rows were removed.

violations.title: `delete_player` counts games then archives-or-deletes in a later query
violations.content:
`delete_player` counts the player's appearances in `games` and `sports_games` (lines 192-197) and then, based on that snapshot, either archives (line 201) or hard-deletes (line 206). A `log_game` or `log_sports_game` request that commits between the count and the delete makes the count stale: the code takes the `deleted: true` branch and the `ON DELETE RESTRICT` FK fires, surfacing exactly the "ugly error" the inline comment says this logic exists to avoid. The response is then a raw Postgres constraint message rather than the intended archive behaviour.

Note the inverse ordering also matters: `log_game` validates `archived` at line 240 and inserts at line 242, so a concurrent archive can still land a game on an archived player.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, move the archive-vs-delete decision for `delete_player` into a single Postgres function (called via `db.rpc`) that locks the player row (`select ... for update`), re-counts references, and archives or deletes within one transaction. As a minimum mitigation, catch a foreign-key violation from the delete at line 206 and fall back to setting `archived: true`, returning `{ archived: true, deleted: false }`.

violations.title: Module-level `data` and `boardId` overwritten by out-of-order `loadBoard` responses
violations.content:
`loadBoard` (line 132) reads the module-level `boardId` and writes the module-level `data` after an `await`, with no guard that `boardId` is still the board the fetch was started for. `switchBoard` sets `boardId` (line 140) and then awaits `loadBoard()`.

If a user switches boards twice in quick succession, both fetches are in flight; whichever resolves last wins. When the first (older board) response arrives second, `data` is set to the old board's payload while `boardId` and the persisted `LAST_BOARD` point at the new board, and `render()` then draws the wrong board's standings under the new board's header. `refresh()` (lines 134-138) has the same exposure — it is invoked from many click handlers (lines 204, 226, 242, 276, 286, 732, 809, 818, 824) that can overlap — and `loadBoards()` additionally reassigns `boardId` from a stale `boards` list.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, guard against out-of-order responses: keep a module-level request token (e.g. `let loadSeq = 0;`), capture `const seq = ++loadSeq;` and `const id = boardId;` at the start of `loadBoard`, and only assign `data = ...` if `seq === loadSeq && id === boardId` when the await resolves. Apply the same token check in `refresh` around the `loadBoards()`/`loadBoard()` pair so a stale refresh cannot clobber newer state.

violations.title: `loadBoard` uses `Promise.all`, so one failing query blanks the entire board
violations.content:
`loadBoard` fans out eight independent REST queries through `Promise.all`. `get` throws on any non-OK response (line 164), and `Promise.all` rejects on the first rejection, so a single failing or missing resource — for example the `padel_sessions` table or the `v_padel_standings` view returning 404/500 on a board that does not even play padel — discards the seven successful responses. The caller in `js/app.js:134-138` catches this and sets `error`, leaving the user with no standings, no games and no player list instead of a board that is merely missing its padel panel.

This is the failure mode where one unrelated query brings down every feature on the screen; the data is naturally partitionable and should degrade per-section.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, change `loadBoard` to use `Promise.allSettled` and map each result to its value or a safe empty fallback (`[]`), so a failure in one query does not discard the others. Keep hard-failing only for the queries the board cannot render without (e.g. `players` and `standings`), and return a per-section error marker for the rest so `js/app.js` can render a partial board with an inline notice instead of an empty screen.
violations.snippet:
const [standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions] = await Promise.all([
    get(`v_standings?select=player_id,name,gp,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_sport_standings?select=sport,player_id,name,games,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&sport=neq.cards&order=name`),
    get(`v_padel_standings?select=player_id,name,archived,rounds,points_for,points_against&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`games?select=id,game_date,p1,p2,p3,p4,loser,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`sports_games?select=id,game_date,sport,a1,a2,b1,b2,score_a,score_b,points_target,session_id,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`players?select=id,name,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_daily_losses?select=player_id,name,losses&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&game_date=eq.${today}`),
    get(`padel_sessions?select=id,game_date,roster,courts,rounds,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=created_at.desc`),
  ]);
  return { standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions };

violations.title: `playLoserSound` never disconnects its Web Audio nodes from the shared context
violations.content: `playLoserSound` creates a `BiquadFilter` (`lp`), an LFO oscillator plus `lfoGain`, and one `OscillatorNode`/`GainNode` pair per note, then connects `lp` to `ctx.destination`. `ctx` is the module-level `audioCtx` created once by `ensureAudio`, so it outlives every call. No node is ever `disconnect()`ed. The source oscillators are stopped and become collectible, but `lp` and `lfoGain` remain wired into the graph (`lp.connect(ctx.destination)` at line 868, `lfoGain.connect(osc.frequency)` at line 883), so each invocation grows the audio graph hanging off the shared destination. Over a long session with many logged games this accumulates filter/gain nodes that are never torn down.
violations.fixPrompt: In `playLoserSound` in `js/app.js`, tear down the audio graph once playback finishes. Track the last note's end time, and on the final oscillator attach an `onended` (or `addEventListener('ended', ...)`) handler that calls `disconnect()` on `lp`, `lfo`, `lfoGain`, and each per-note `osc`/`g` pair. Keep the existing `try`/`catch` so a missing-audio environment still degrades silently.

violations.title: `showPecundang` drops the previous toast without clearing its pending `setTimeout`
violations.content: `showPecundang` removes any existing toast with `document.querySelector('.pecundang')?.remove()` at line 897, but that bypasses the previous invocation's `close`, so the earlier `timer = setTimeout(close, 4200)` (line 910) is never cleared. The stale timer keeps the old closure — and through it the detached toast element and its `onUndo` callback — alive until it fires, at which point it calls `o.remove()` on an already-detached node. Only the `clearTimeout` inside `close` cleans this up, and that path is skipped when the toast is replaced rather than closed. Two games logged within 4.2 seconds of each other reproduce it.
violations.fixPrompt: In `showPecundang` in `js/app.js`, keep the pending timeout id in a module-level variable (e.g. `pecundangTimer`) instead of a purely local one. At the top of the function, call `clearTimeout(pecundangTimer)` alongside the existing `document.querySelector('.pecundang')?.remove()` so replacing a toast also cancels the previous timer, and have `close` clear that same variable.

violations.title: `listLeaderboards` returns a raw array in mock mode but a Promise otherwise
violations.content: `listLeaderboards` is declared as a plain arrow function whose two branches return different kinds of value: when `USE_MOCK` is true it returns the synchronous array produced by `mock.listLeaderboards()`, and otherwise it returns the Promise returned by `get(...)`. The return type is therefore `Array | Promise<Array>` depending on a module-level flag. It happens to work today only because every caller (`loadBoards` in `js/app.js`) awaits the result, and `await` on a non-thenable is a no-op. Any caller that treats the result synchronously (or that chains `.then`/`.catch` on it) would break in exactly one of the two modes, and the mock branch silently swallows the possibility of rejection handling. The same shape is repeated in every exported wrapper in this file.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, make the mock and live branches return the same wrapped type. Either declare `listLeaderboards` as `async` (so the mock branch is auto-wrapped in a Promise), or wrap the mock branch explicitly with `Promise.resolve(...)`. Apply the same treatment to the other exported wrappers (`createLeaderboard`, `renameLeaderboard`, `deleteLeaderboard`, `addPlayer`, `deletePlayer`, `restorePlayer`, `logGame`, `undoLast`, `editLoser`, `deleteGame`, `logSportsGame`, `createPadelSession`, `undoLastSports`, `editSportsScore`, `deleteSportsGame`) so every export consistently returns a Promise.
violations.snippet:
export const listLeaderboards = () =>
  USE_MOCK ? mock.listLeaderboards() : get('leaderboards?select=id,name,game_types,points_target&order=name');

violations.title: `logSportsGame` returns either a plain object or a Promise depending on `USE_MOCK`
violations.content: `logSportsGame` explicitly returns the result of a ternary whose branches have different types: `mock.logSportsGame(...)` returns the newly created game object synchronously, while `call('log_sports_game', ...)` returns a Promise resolving to the server row. Callers such as the `save` handler in `openLogSport` and the round-runner's log handler in `js/app.js` pass this through `attempt(...)`, which awaits it — so failures in the mock branch would throw synchronously at call time rather than rejecting, and error handling differs between the two modes. A function that sometimes returns a wrapped value and sometimes the raw value is easy to misuse as the codebase grows.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, mark `logSportsGame` as `async` (or wrap the mock branch in `Promise.resolve(...)`) so both branches return a Promise resolving to the created sports-game row, regardless of `USE_MOCK`.

violations.title: Mock `renameLeaderboard` returns `undefined` when the board id is unknown
violations.content: `renameLeaderboard` in the mock backend does `const b = board(id); if (b) { ... } return b;` — so when `board(id)` finds no matching board it returns `undefined`, while the success path returns the mutated board object and the live path (`call('rename_leaderboard', ...)`) resolves to a server row. The caller in `openRenameBoard` (`js/app.js`) treats any non-throwing result as success, so a rename against a stale or deleted `boardId` in mock mode silently reports success and closes the sheet even though nothing was renamed. Mixing a real object with an implicit `undefined` hides this failure instead of surfacing it as an error.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, make the mock `renameLeaderboard` fail loudly instead of returning `undefined`: if `board(id)` is falsy, `throw new Error('that leaderboard no longer exists')`; otherwise apply the updates and return the board object, so the return type is always a board (or a thrown error) — matching the live `call('rename_leaderboard', ...)` path.

violations.title: `undo_last` returns `data: null` on one branch and a game object on the other
violations.content: The `undo_last` case resolves its success payload to two different shapes: when there is no game to undo it returns `ok(null)` (line 257), giving the caller `{ ok: true, data: null }`; on the normal path it returns `ok(last)` (line 261), giving `{ ok: true, data: { id: number } }`. Both are `ok: true` responses, so a client that treats a successful response as "a game was deleted" and reads `data.id` will throw on an empty board. The no-op case is also indistinguishable from a real deletion without an extra null check, which the sibling `delete_game` / `delete_sports_game` handlers never require because they always return an object. A consistent contract — e.g. always returning `{ game_id: last?.id ?? null, deleted: !!last }` — would let callers use one code path.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `undo_last` case return a consistently shaped success payload. Replace `return ok(null)` (the `if (!last)` branch) and `return ok(last)` with a single object shape, e.g. `return ok({ game_id: null, deleted: false })` when there is nothing to undo and `return ok({ game_id: last.id, deleted: true })` after a successful delete. Update any front-end callers of the `undo_last` action that currently read `data` or `data.id` directly so they read the new fields.

violations.title: `undo_last_sports` returns `data: null` on one branch and a game object on the other
violations.content: Same inconsistency as `undo_last`: the `undo_last_sports` case returns `ok(null)` at line 353 when no sports game exists, and `ok(last)` (an object `{ id }`) at line 357 after deleting one. Both are `ok: true`, so callers cannot distinguish "nothing to undo" from "undo succeeded" without a null guard, and any code that reads `data.id` off a successful response will throw when the board has no logged rounds.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `undo_last_sports` case return one consistent success shape instead of mixing `null` and an object. Return e.g. `ok({ sports_game_id: null, deleted: false })` in the `if (!last)` branch and `ok({ sports_game_id: last.id, deleted: true })` after the delete succeeds, and update front-end callers of the `undo_last_sports` action accordingly.

violations.title: `mapGames` matches schedule slots to games with a nested scan instead of a hash map
violations.content: `mapGames` iterates every scheduled match and, for each one, runs `sgames.find(...)` over the entire list of logged session games — an O(matches × games) nested loop. Worse, each candidate comparison allocates two fresh `Set`s via `setOf([x.a1, x.a2])` / `setOf([x.b1, x.b2])` and then compares them with `eq`, so the per-comparison cost includes repeated allocation and spreading. Because `draw()` calls `mapGames(sessionGames(session.id))` and `draw()` re-runs after every single round is logged, this quadratic work is repeated on each score entry during an Americano night. Keying the logged games once into a `Map` (canonical key = the sorted player ids of both sides, computed once per game) turns the whole pass into a linear lookup.
violations.fixPrompt: In `mapGames` in `js/app.js`, precompute a `Map` from logged games instead of scanning with `.find()`. Build a canonical key for each game once — e.g. `const key = (s1, s2) => [s1.slice().sort((x,y)=>x-y).join(','), s2.slice().sort((x,y)=>x-y).join(',')].sort().join('|')` applied to `[x.a1,x.a2].filter(v=>v!=null)` and `[x.b1,x.b2].filter(v=>v!=null)` — and store `orientationKey -> game` in a `Map`. Then for each schedule slot compute the same key from `mt.a`/`mt.b` and do a single `Map.get`, skipping entries already in `used`. This removes both the nested scan and the per-comparison `Set` allocations while keeping the existing orientation-insensitive matching behaviour.

violations.title: `rowsHTML` recomputes `losingStreak` over the full games array once per player row
violations.content: `rowsHTML` calls `losingStreak(data?.games ?? [], p.player_id)` inside the per-player `.map()`, so the entire `data.games` array is rescanned from scratch for every row rendered. With the ranked and unranked lists both passed through `rowsHTML` (lines 1121 and 1123), this is O(players × games) on every `render()` — and `render()` runs after every board switch, mode toggle, and write. A single pass over `data.games` building a `Map<player_id, streak>` would give O(games + players) and O(1) per row.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, compute losing streaks once per render instead of per row. Add a helper that walks `data.games` a single time (newest-first, as `losingStreak` already assumes) and returns a `Map` of `player_id -> streak`, then pass that map into `rowsHTML` (and thread it through `tableHTML`) so each row does a `streaks.get(p.player_id) ?? 0` lookup rather than calling `losingStreak` again.

violations.title: `nameOf` does a linear `players.find()` and is called inside every row-rendering loop
violations.content: `nameOf` resolves a player id with `data?.players.find(...)`, an O(players) scan, and it is invoked from inside render loops rather than once: `cardRow` calls it 5× per card game (line 761 and line 763), `sportRow` calls it up to 8× per racquet game (lines 777–780), and `openGames`'s `draw()` maps it over every merged game (line 799). The result is O(games × players) linear scans each time the Recent games sheet redraws — and it redraws after every edit or delete. A `Map<id, name>` rebuilt whenever `data` changes would make each lookup O(1).

'?'`. Keep the same `'?'` fallback so callers are unaffected.

violations.title: Mock `standings` re-filters the whole games list for every player
violations.content: `standings` calls `gamesOf(id)` inside the per-player `.map()`, so `s.games` is filtered from scratch once per player, and each retained game is then re-scanned with `played.filter(...)`. On top of that, `inGame` builds a throwaway `[g.p1, g.p2, g.p3, g.p4]` array and uses `.includes` for every (player, game) pair. The whole thing is O(players × games) with heavy per-pair allocation, and `standings(id)` runs on every `mock.loadBoard` — i.e. every refresh in demo mode. A single pass over the board's games accumulating counts into a `Map<player_id, {gp, losses}>` is linear.

Then map the board's players over that `Map`, defaulting to zeros, and keep the existing `localeCompare` sort and returned row shape.

violations.title: `cleanGameTypes` does an O(n×m) array scan with `GAME_TYPES.includes` inside a `.filter`
violations.content:
`GAME_TYPES` is a plain array (line 65) and `cleanGameTypes` calls `GAME_TYPES.includes(t)` once per element of the caller-supplied array inside `.filter` (line 70), giving an O(n×m) nested scan where a `Set` lookup would be O(1) per element.

The constant list is only 6 entries, so the constant factor is small — but `payload.game_types` is unvalidated client input of arbitrary length, reached on the `create_leaderboard` and `rename_leaderboard` paths (lines 140, 156) before any size check. A client sending a large array makes this scan proportional to `n × 6` string comparisons on the Edge Function's single-threaded event loop. Since `GAME_TYPES` is a module-level constant, hoisting it to a `Set` built once at load makes the membership check O(1) with no per-request cost. The neighbouring `SPORTS.includes(sport)` check (line 289) is a single lookup, not a loop, so it does not need the same treatment.

This is a small win, not a hot-path emergency — worth taking because the fix is a one-line constant change with no behavioural difference (the elements are strings, so `Set` membership matches `Array.includes` semantics exactly).

violations.title: `loadBoard` fetches four aggregate views over data it already fetches raw
violations.content:
`loadBoard` issues eight parallel requests, but four of them (`v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, `v_daily_losses`) are pure aggregations of rows that the same `Promise.all` already downloads in full: `games`, `sports_games`, and `players`.

The mock backend in this very file proves the derivation is trivial and lossless — `standings` (line 52), `sportStandings` (line 62), `padelStandings` (line 82), and `dailyLosses` (line 75) each compute the identical shape from `s.games` / `s.sportsGames` / `s.players`, and the comments state they mirror the SQL views exactly.

Because the raw history is transferred anyway, the four view requests buy no bandwidth savings; they only add four extra HTTP requests (four extra TLS/PostgREST round trips, four extra query plans over the same base tables) on every board load. They are parallelized, so the wall-clock penalty is bounded by the slowest request rather than the sum — which is why this is low rather than high — but on a mobile connection the per-request overhead and connection contention are still real, and every one of these responses is recomputable from data already in hand.

This is a deliberate server-side-aggregation design, so it is a tradeoff rather than a plain bug. The tradeoff stops paying off precisely when the client also pulls the unaggregated rows, which is the case here.
violations.fixPrompt: In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, drop the `v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, and `v_daily_losses` requests from the `Promise.all`, reducing it to the three base fetches (`games`, `sports_games`, `players`) plus `padel_sessions`. Then derive the four removed values client-side from those rows, reusing the logic already written for the mock backend in the same file: `standings` (line 52), `sportStandings` (line 62), `padelStandings` (line 82), and `dailyLosses` (line 75). Lift those four helpers out of the `mock` IIFE into module-level pure functions that take `(games, sportsGames, players)` instead of reading the closed-over `s`, so both the mock path and the real path call the same code. Keep the returned object shape of `loadBoard` byte-for-byte identical (`{ standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions }`) with the same field names and the same `order=name` sort ordering so no caller changes. Verify the derived output matches the SQL views for a board with archived players, singles and doubles racquet games, and padel rounds; if any view applies filtering or ordering the client logic does not reproduce (e.g. the `sport=neq.cards` filter on `v_sport_standings`), replicate it in the client function.

violations.title: Client config mixes a copied config file, hostname sniffing, and a URL query param
violations.content:
`js/config.js` derives runtime settings from at least three different mechanisms in one small module: a checked-out copy of `js/config.example.js` (the file itself, holding literal values such as the Supabase URL/key), a hardcoded hostname allowlist (`['localhost', '127.0.0.1'].includes(...)`) used to infer the environment, and a URL query parameter (`new URLSearchParams(globalThis.location?.search ?? '').has(...)`) used to toggle mock mode.

Meanwhile the server side (`supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`) reads every setting from the environment via `Deno.env.get` (`ALLOWED_ORIGIN`, service keys, passcode). So the same application has two unrelated configuration systems, and within the browser half there is no single source of truth: whether the app talks to a real backend depends on which host it happens to be served from and on an ad-hoc query string, not on one declared setting.

This matters because environment inference by hostname silently breaks on any host not in the literal list (preview deploys, LAN IPs, custom dev domains), and because `config.js` is a manual copy of `config.example.js` — the two drift with no mechanism to detect a missing or stale key.
violations.fixPrompt: Unify client configuration in `js/config.js` into a single explicit config object with one declared source of truth per setting. Replace the hostname allowlist check (`['localhost', '127.0.0.1'].includes(...)`) and the query-param toggle (`new URLSearchParams(...).has(...)`) with an explicit exported flag (e.g. `USE_MOCK`) whose value is set in the config file itself, or injected at build time, rather than inferred from `location.hostname`. Keep the query param only as a documented developer override that reads the same named key. Add a startup validation step that asserts every key present in `js/config.example.js` also exists in `js/config.js`, and throws a clear error naming the missing key, so the example file and the real file cannot drift silently.

violations.title: Backend selected by sniffing the hostname at runtime
violations.content: Which Supabase project the app talks to is decided by an inline hostname check: `const isLocal = ['localhost', '127.0.0.1'].includes(globalThis.location?.hostname); const active = isLocal ? LOCAL : PROD;`. The environment is inferred from where the page happens to be served rather than from an explicit configuration value, and the branch fails open to production. violations.title: Client config mixes a copied config file, hostname sniffing, and a URL query param
violations.content:
`js/config.js` derives runtime settings from at least three different mechanisms in one small module: a checked-out copy of `js/config.example.js` (the file itself, holding literal values such as the Supabase URL/key), a hardcoded hostname allowlist (`['localhost', '127.0.0.1'].includes(...)`) used to infer the environment, and a URL query parameter (`new URLSearchParams(globalThis.location?.search ?? '').has(...)`) used to toggle mock mode.

Meanwhile the server side (`supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`) reads every setting from the environment via `Deno.env.get` (`ALLOWED_ORIGIN`, service keys, passcode). So the same application has two unrelated configuration systems, and within the browser half there is no single source of truth: whether the app talks to a real backend depends on which host it happens to be served from and on an ad-hoc query string, not on one declared setting.

This matters because environment inference by hostname silently breaks on any host not in the literal list (preview deploys, LAN IPs, custom dev domains), and because `config.js` is a manual copy of `config.example.js` — the two drift with no mechanism to detect a missing or stale key.
violations.fixPrompt: Unify client configuration in `js/config.js` into a single explicit config object with one declared source of truth per setting. Replace the hostname allowlist check (`['localhost', '127.0.0.1'].includes(...)`) and the query-param toggle (`new URLSearchParams(...).has(...)`) with an explicit exported flag (e.g. `USE_MOCK`) whose value is set in the config file itself, or injected at build time, rather than inferred from `location.hostname`. Keep the query param only as a documented developer override that reads the same named key. Add a startup validation step that asserts every key present in `js/config.example.js` also exists in `js/config.js`, and throws a clear error naming the missing key, so the example file and the real file cannot drift silently.

violations.title: Backend selected by sniffing the hostname at runtime
violations.content: Which Supabase project the app talks to is decided by an inline hostname check: `const isLocal = ['localhost', '127.0.0.1'].includes(globalThis.location?.hostname); const active = isLocal ? LOCAL : PROD;`. The environment is inferred from where the page happens to be served rather than from an explicit configuration value, and the branch fails open to production. Any host that is not literally `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` silently gets the live project — a LAN IP such as `192.168.1.x` when testing from a phone, `[::1]`, a `*.local` mDNS name, or a staging deployment. There is also no way to point a locally served page at production (or the reverse) for a deliberate smoke test without editing the file. `js/config.example.js:21-22` carries the identical pattern, so the template propagates it to every copy.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/config.js`, replace the hostname sniff with an explicit target selection: define a named map of environments (e.g. `const ENVS = { local: LOCAL, prod: PROD }`) and pick from it using an explicit override first — for example a `?env=local` URL parameter or a `globalThis.LOTD_ENV` value set by the page — falling back to the hostname heuristic only as a default. Keep the failure mode conservative and make the chosen environment visible (e.g. export it as `ACTIVE_ENV`) so it can be asserted in tests. Apply the same change to `js/config.example.js` so new copies inherit it.
violations.snippet:
const isLocal = ['localhost', '127.0.0.1'].includes(globalThis.location?.hostname);
const active = isLocal ? LOCAL : PROD;

`js/api.js` imports `./config.js` (for the mock toggle) but then defines domain configuration inline rather than sourcing it from that module: `ALL_TYPES = ['cards', 'tt_singles', 'tt_doubles', 'padel']` and the default `points_target: 21`, with the same `21` repeated later as an inline fallback in `logSportsGame` (`board(leaderboard_id)?.points_target ?? 21`).

violations.title: `get` performs Supabase REST reads with no retry on transient failures
violations.content: `get` is the shared read primitive for every Supabase REST call in the app, but the single `fetch` has no retry wrapper. Any transient condition — a dropped connection, DNS blip, mobile network handoff, or a `502`/`503`/`429` from the Supabase edge — throws immediately and surfaces to the user as "Couldn't reach the server". Because this is a `GET` with no side effects, retrying is fully safe and idempotent, so this is the highest-value place to add backoff: a couple of retries would absorb the majority of these failures invisibly. The current code also collapses the distinction between retryable (`5xx`, `429`, network error) and non-retryable (`4xx`) responses.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, add retry-with-exponential-backoff to `get`. Wrap the `fetch` call in a loop of ~3 attempts. Retry when `fetch` itself rejects (network error) or when `res.status` is `429` or >= `500`; do not retry other `4xx` statuses — throw those immediately. Back off between attempts (e.g. 300ms, 600ms, 1200ms) with a small random jitter, and honour the `Retry-After` header if present on a `429`. After the final attempt, throw the existing `Couldn't reach the server (${res.status})` error so callers are unaffected. Consider extracting the retry loop into a small `fetchWithRetry` helper so it can be reused.
violations.snippet:
const res = await fetch(`${SUPABASE_URL}/rest/v1/${path}`, { headers: H });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Couldn't reach the server (${res.status})`);

violations.title: `call` invokes the admin edge function with no retry on transient failures
violations.content:
`call` is the single entry point for every admin action against the `ADMIN_FN` edge function, and it issues one `fetch` with no retry. Edge functions are especially prone to transient failures — cold starts, worker recycling, and boot timeouts routinely produce `503`/`504` responses that succeed on an immediate retry. Today any such blip fails the user's admin action outright.

Unlike `get`, this is a `POST` that mutates state, so a blanket retry is not safe: an action that actually applied server-side but whose response was lost would be applied twice. Retries here should be limited to cases where the request provably did not reach the handler — a `fetch` rejection or a `503`/`504` — or the actions should be made idempotent (e.g. a client-generated request id the handler de-duplicates on) before retrying more broadly.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, add narrow retry logic to `call`. Retry only on conditions where the request almost certainly did not apply server-side: a `fetch` rejection before any response, or `res.status` of `503`/`504`. Do not retry on other `5xx`, on `4xx`, or on a well-formed response where `out.ok` is false, since the mutation may have partially applied. Use ~2 retries with exponential backoff (e.g. 300ms then 900ms) plus jitter. For stronger safety, generate a unique request id per `call` invocation, include it in the JSON body, and de-duplicate on it in the admin edge function handler so retries become fully idempotent; only widen the retry conditions once that de-duplication is in place. Preserve the existing error messages and return value.

violations.title: `loadBoard` aborts the whole board load if any one of eight independent queries fails
violations.content:
`loadBoard` fetches eight independent datasets (`v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, `games`, `sports_games`, `players`, `v_daily_losses`, `padel_sessions`) with `Promise.all`. A single rejection — a transient network error, a permissions issue on one view, or a missing/renamed table such as `padel_sessions` on a board that never plays padel — rejects the whole call, so the caller sees a total load failure and the UI renders nothing.

These sections are independent: card standings do not depend on padel sessions, and the daily-loss panel does not depend on the sports game log. The batch should report partial success so the sections that did load still render, with only the failed section showing an error or empty state.
violations.fixPrompt: In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, replace `Promise.all` with `Promise.allSettled` over the eight `get(...)` calls. Map each settled result to its `value` on fulfilment and to a safe empty default (`[]`) on rejection, and collect the rejection reasons into an `errors` field on the returned object (e.g. `{ standings, sportStandings, ..., errors }`) so callers can surface a per-section warning instead of failing the entire board render. Keep the existing `USE_MOCK` short-circuit and the returned property names unchanged so existing consumers keep working.
violations.snippet:
const [standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions] = await Promise.all([
    get(`v_standings?select=player_id,name,gp,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_sport_standings?select=sport,player_id,name,games,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&sport=neq.cards&order=name`),
    get(`v_padel_standings?select=player_id,name,archived,rounds,points_for,points_against&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`games?select=id,game_date,p1,p2,p3,p4,loser,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`sports_games?select=id,game_date,sport,a1,a2,b1,b2,score_a,score_b,points_target,session_id,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`players?select=id,name,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_daily_losses?select=player_id,name,losses&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&game_date=eq.${today}`),
    get(`padel_sessions?select=id,game_date,roster,courts,rounds,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=created_at.desc`),
  ]);
  return { standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions };

violations.title: `loadBoard` fetches unbounded `games` and `sports_games` history with no `limit`
violations.content:
The `games` and `sports_games` queries inside `loadBoard` specify `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc` but no `limit` or range header, so every call materializes the board's **entire** game history into an in-memory array. This collection has no size cap and grows monotonically for the life of the leaderboard.

The growth is amplified by how often it runs: `refresh()` calls `loadBoard()` and is invoked after every single write — every logged card game, every racquet game, and notably after *each individual match* in the Americano round-runner (`openSessionRunner` calls `await refresh(); draw();` on each `Log` tap). So a single padel night re-downloads and re-parses the full history dozens of times, each time larger than the last.

Downstream consumers hold the whole array too: `openGames()` builds `merged()` from all of `data.games` plus all of `data.sportsGames` and writes every row into `rows.innerHTML` in one shot, and `rowsHTML` calls `losingStreak(data?.games ?? [], p.player_id)` once per player over the full array. On a long-lived board viewed from a phone, the unbounded payload plus the unbounded DOM render is the realistic memory/latency failure point.

Add server-side pagination (a `limit` on the initial load, with an explicit "load more" for the history sheet) so the in-memory collection has a bounded size independent of how long the board has existed.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, bound the two history queries so the in-memory arrays cannot grow without limit. Add an explicit `limit` to the `games` and `sports_games` PostgREST queries (e.g. `&limit=200`), since both already sort newest-first via `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`. Introduce a named constant such as `HISTORY_LIMIT` at module scope rather than inlining the number.

Then make the truncation visible instead of silent: have `openGames()` in `js/app.js` render a "Load older games" affordance when the returned page is full (length === HISTORY_LIMIT), fetching the next page via a new paginated read helper that accepts an offset. Ensure the mock backend in `api.js` honours the same limit so demo mode matches production behaviour.

Also confirm that the aggregate views (`v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, `v_daily_losses`) are still the source of truth for all standings numbers, so limiting the raw game arrays cannot change any displayed ranking. The one place that consumes raw `data.games` for a computed value is `losingStreak` in `rowsHTML` — verify a truncated array still yields a correct streak, or cap the streak computation explicitly.

violations.title: Front end `app.js` has no client-side error reporting
violations.content:
`js/app.js` is the entire UI layer — it imports `./api.js`, `./export.mjs`, `./ranking.mjs`, and `./americano.mjs`, and drives the DOM directly (`document.createElement`, `box.querySelectorAll`, `r.addEventListener`). No error tracking SDK is imported here or in any sibling module, and there is no visible `globalThis.addEventListener('error', ...)` or `'unhandledrejection'` registration.

Every network call goes through `./api.js`, so a rejected fetch inside an event handler such as the `r.addEventListener` wiring becomes an unhandled rejection that the user sees only as a button that silently does nothing. Since this is a static client app with no server-rendered error page, there is no other channel through which such a failure could reach the maintainer.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, register global handlers early in module initialization: `globalThis.addEventListener('error', ...)` and `globalThis.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', ...)`, forwarding the error to an error tracking service. Gate initialization on a DSN value exported from `js/config.js` (and add the matching placeholder key to `js/config.example.js`) so that the mock/local mode driven by `USE_MOCK` does not report. As a minimum fallback if no external service is desired, surface these failures in the UI instead of letting them vanish.
violations.snippet: import * as api from './api.js';

violations.title: `rosterMem` is a module-level cache with no size limit or eviction policy
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a module-scoped object used as a cache of the last-used A/B roster split, keyed by `${boardId}:${sport}` and written on every successful racquet save (`rosterMem[memKey()] = { a: [...a], b: [...b] }` in the `save` handler of `openLogSport`). Entries are only ever added — nothing removes them, and there is no maximum entry count.

In practice the key space is bounded by (number of boards) × (5 sports), and each value holds at most four integer ids, so this will not realistically exhaust memory in a browser tab. It is flagged as a hygiene issue rather than a crash risk: the cache also never invalidates when a board is deleted via `openDeleteBoard`, so stale roster entries for deleted boards persist for the lifetime of the page.

A bounded structure with explicit eviction would make the growth characteristics obvious and drop entries for boards that no longer exist.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `js/app.js`, convert `rosterMem` from a bare object into a bounded LRU-style cache. Replace it with a `Map` (which preserves insertion order) and add a small helper that, on write, deletes the existing key before re-inserting it and then evicts the oldest entry while `size` exceeds a named constant such as `ROSTER_MEM_MAX` (a value like 20 is ample). Update the read in `restore()` and the write in the `save` handler of `openLogSport` to use `.get()`/`.set()` through that helper.

Additionally, clear entries for a deleted board: in `openDeleteBoard`, after the delete succeeds, remove every `rosterMem` key whose `boardId` prefix matches the deleted board so stale rosters do not survive the board itself.

const rosterMem = {};   // `${boardId}:${sport}` -> { a:[ids], b:[ids] }

violations.title: Module-level `data` cache is only refreshed on local writes, so remote changes and the date rollover never invalidate it
violations.content:
`data` (declared at line 49) holds the entire board payload — `standings`, `games`, `sportsGames`, `players`, `dailyLosses`, `padelSessions` — and is only repopulated by `loadBoard()` when `refresh()` or `switchBoard()` is called. Both are triggered exclusively by local user actions (initial `refresh()` at line 1221, a board switch, or a successful write from this tab). There is no TTL, no polling, no revalidation on `visibilitychange`/`focus`, and no realtime subscription to Supabase.

This is a shared leaderboard: several people log games from their own devices against the same `leaderboards` row. A tab left open shows stale standings indefinitely — every render path (`spotlightHTML`, `sportTablesHTML`, `padelTableHTML`, `padelSessionBanner`, `openGames`) reads from this snapshot.

The staleness is also time-based, not just write-based: `api.loadBoard()` resolves `localToday()` once at fetch time and filters `v_daily_losses` on `game_date=eq.<today>` (`js/api.js:179` and `js/api.js:187`). A tab open across midnight keeps rendering yesterday's row under the "Today's biggest loser" heading, while `padelSpotlightHTML` (line 1013) recomputes today's padel loser against a freshly-evaluated `api.localToday()` — so the two spotlights disagree about what "today" means.

The Americano round-runner is the worst case: `openSessionRunner` can stay open for a whole padel night while another phone logs rounds into the same `session_id`, and the live "tonight" standings silently omit them.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, add an invalidation strategy for the module-level `data` cache. At minimum: (1) record the fetch time alongside `data` in `loadBoard()`, and re-run `refresh()` on `document.visibilitychange` / `window.focus` when the snapshot is older than a short TTL (e.g. 30–60s); (2) also invalidate when `api.localToday()` no longer matches the date captured at fetch time, so the "Today's biggest loser" spotlight and `dailyLosses` do not survive a midnight rollover; (3) for `openSessionRunner`, poll `refresh()` + `draw()` on an interval (or subscribe to Supabase realtime on `sports_games`) while the runner sheet is open, clearing the interval in the sheet's close handler.

violations.title: `rosterMem` grows without bound and is never cleared when its board or players are removed
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a plain object cache keyed `${boardId}:${sport}` holding the last A/B roster split, written in `openLogSport`'s save handler (line 532) and read by `restore()` (lines 429–434). Nothing ever deletes an entry: not `openDeleteBoard` (which deletes the board and all its players), not `deletePlayer`/`restorePlayer`, not `switchBoard`.

`restore()` does filter out ids missing from `activePlayers()`, which prevents deleted players leaking into the picker, so the user-visible impact is limited. What remains is an entry-per-board-per-sport that accumulates for the lifetime of the page — including entries keyed to boards that no longer exist — and a subtle behavioural quirk: a player archived and later restored silently reappears pre-selected in the roster from a session logged before they were archived.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, invalidate `rosterMem` entries when their source data disappears: delete all keys starting with `${boardId}:` inside `openDeleteBoard`'s success branch, and drop the cached ids for a player in the `deletePlayer` handler in `openPlayers`. Alternatively store the roster memory with a timestamp and treat entries older than the current session (or older than a few hours) as expired inside `restore()`.

violations.title: Edge function `admin` has no error monitoring integration
violations.content:
The only import in this module is `https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2` — there is no Sentry, Bugsnag, Datadog, or OpenTelemetry SDK initialized. This is the sole server-side entry point of the application: it registers a handler via `Deno.serve` and fans out to database work (`Promise.all`), passcode verification (`crypto.subtle.digest`, `passcodeMatches`), and rate limiting (`fails.get`, `Date.now`). The visible error path consists only of the local `bad` and `json` helpers, which shape an HTTP response for the caller and report nothing outbound.

Because of that, a failure inside any handler branch — a Supabase query error, a malformed payload that slips past the `/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/` and `Number.isInteger` guards, or an unhandled promise rejection inside `Promise.all` — surfaces to the user as a status code and then disappears. Deno Deploy captures stderr, but nothing aggregates, alerts on, or de-duplicates these, so a regression affecting every write request looks identical to normal operation from the outside.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, add error monitoring around the `Deno.serve` handler. Wrap the top-level handler body in a try/catch that reports the caught error to an external service before returning the existing `bad(...)` response, and register a global `unhandledrejection` listener that reports as well. Use a Deno-compatible SDK (for example `https://esm.sh/@sentry/deno`) initialized from a `SENTRY_DSN` read via `Deno.env.get`, and skip initialization when the variable is absent so local runs are unaffected. Include the request path and the resolved action name as context on each report, but do not attach the passcode or any hashed credential material.

violations.title: HTTP handler `Deno.serve` has no response time or query duration instrumentation
violations.content:
The `Deno.serve` handler in this module is the application's only HTTP server, and no metrics library (`prom-client`, StatsD, OpenTelemetry) appears among its imports — the sole import is `https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2`. The visible call list shows `Date.now` used only for rate-limit bookkeeping alongside `fails.get`, not for timing.

As a result, request latency is unmeasured, and the Supabase queries this function issues — including the fan-out under `Promise.all` and the aggregate reads backing the standings views — have no recorded duration. A query that degrades as the games and sports games tables grow, or a slow `crypto.subtle.digest` path under load, will not be visible until requests start timing out.
violations.fixPrompt: Instrument the `Deno.serve` handler in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts` with timing: capture a start timestamp at the top of the handler, and on every exit path (including the `bad` error responses) record the elapsed duration together with the action name and response status. Also time the Supabase calls, especially the ones batched under `Promise.all`. Emit these either through an OpenTelemetry exporter or, if a full metrics backend is out of scope, as structured single-line records that Deno Deploy log ingestion can aggregate. Keep the instrumentation off the hot path when a metrics endpoint is not configured.
