violations.title: Rate-limit map `fails` grows without bound and has no eviction
violations.content:
`fails` is a module-level `Map` keyed by client IP that acts as an in-memory cache for the brute-force lockout, but it has no size cap, no TTL sweep, and no eviction policy. An entry is added on every failed passcode attempt (`fails.set(ip, ...)`, line 124) and is only ever removed on a *successful* passcode (`fails.delete(ip)`, line 128). Entries whose `until` timestamp has already expired are never reclaimed — the lockout check at line 116 reads `rec.until > now` but leaves the stale record in place, so the map only grows for the lifetime of the Edge Function instance.

The key is derived from the `x-forwarded-for` header (line 113), which is request-controlled. Anyone who can reach the function can send POSTs with a wrong passcode and a fresh spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` value each time, inserting an unbounded number of distinct keys — and the per-IP lockout never engages, because every request lands on a brand-new key. Each entry is small, but with no upper bound the map grows linearly with request volume until the isolate hits its memory limit and the function crashes, taking down the only write path for the app.

Even without a malicious actor, ordinary traffic from many distinct client IPs (mobile networks rotate addresses) accumulates entries indefinitely, since only successfully-authenticated IPs are ever deleted.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, bound the in-memory `fails` map so it cannot grow without limit.

1. Add a `MAX_TRACKED = 10_000` (or similar) constant alongside `MAX_FAILS` and `LOCK_MS`.
2. Store a `seen: number` timestamp on each record so counters that never reached `MAX_FAILS` can be aged out.
3. Before inserting a new entry in the failure path (`fails.set(ip, ...)` near line 124), sweep expired records: iterate `fails` and `delete` any entry whose `until` is `0` or `<= now` and whose `seen` is older than `LOCK_MS`.
4. After the sweep, if `fails.size >= MAX_TRACKED`, evict the oldest entries (or clear the map) before adding the new one, so the map has a hard ceiling regardless of traffic.
5. Also `fails.delete(ip)` in the lockout check around line 116 when `rec.until <= now`, so expired lockouts are reclaimed on read as well.

Keep the existing behaviour otherwise: 5 wrong passcodes still triggers a 60s cooldown, and a correct passcode still clears the counter.
violations.snippet: const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>();

violations.title: Lockout counter in `fails` is never invalidated when its window expires
violations.content:
The in-memory `fails` map stores `{ n, until }` per IP, but the failure count `n` is only ever cleared on a *successful* passcode (`fails.delete(ip)` on line 128). When the lockout window at line 116 (`rec.until > now`) elapses, the stale `n` value survives — nothing resets it. On the next wrong passcode, line 123 computes `n = (rec?.n ?? 0) + 1`, which is already `>= MAX_FAILS`, so line 124 immediately re-locks the IP for another `LOCK_MS`.

The practical effect: once an IP crosses 5 failures, a single mistyped passcode at any later point — hours or days later — triggers a fresh 60s lockout, because the counter is stale cached state that never expires alongside the `until` timestamp it is paired with. The intended "5 wrong passcodes -> 60s cooldown" behaviour silently degrades into "1 wrong passcode -> 60s cooldown, forever" for that IP. For a shared-NAT friend group all hitting the same egress IP, one person's typo locks out everyone.

The fix is to treat an expired `until` as an invalidation signal and restart the count from zero.

violations.title: `fails` map has no eviction, so expired entries accumulate unboundedly
violations.content:
`const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>()` retains an entry per distinct client IP for the lifetime of the function instance. Entries are removed only on a successful passcode (line 128); an IP that fails once and never returns leaves its record in the map permanently. The `until` field encodes an expiry for the *lockout*, but nothing ever sweeps entries whose `until` has passed.

Each record is small, so this is not an immediate risk for a friend-group app on a warm instance, but the map is fed directly from the attacker-controlled `x-forwarded-for` header (line 113). A stream of requests with varied `X-Forwarded-For` values inserts an unbounded number of never-collected keys, and the retained stale entries are also what make the counter bug above persist indefinitely. A periodic or opportunistic sweep of records whose `until` has elapsed bounds the memory and gives the cached state a real expiry.
violations.snippet: const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>();

violations.title: `get` performs Supabase REST reads with no retry on transient failures
violations.content: `get` is the shared read primitive for every Supabase REST call in the app, but the single `fetch` has no retry wrapper. Any transient condition — a dropped connection, DNS blip, mobile network handoff, or a `502`/`503`/`429` from the Supabase edge — throws immediately and surfaces to the user as "Couldn't reach the server". Because this is a `GET` with no side effects, retrying is fully safe and idempotent, so this is the highest-value place to add backoff: a couple of retries would absorb the majority of these failures invisibly. The current code also collapses the distinction between retryable (`5xx`, `429`, network error) and non-retryable (`4xx`) responses.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, add retry-with-exponential-backoff to `get`. Wrap the `fetch` call in a loop of ~3 attempts. Retry when `fetch` itself rejects (network error) or when `res.status` is `429` or >= `500`; do not retry other `4xx` statuses — throw those immediately. Back off between attempts (e.g. 300ms, 600ms, 1200ms) with a small random jitter, and honour the `Retry-After` header if present on a `429`. After the final attempt, throw the existing `Couldn't reach the server (${res.status})` error so callers are unaffected. Consider extracting the retry loop into a small `fetchWithRetry` helper so it can be reused.
violations.snippet:
const res = await fetch(`${SUPABASE_URL}/rest/v1/${path}`, { headers: H });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Couldn't reach the server (${res.status})`);

violations.title: `call` invokes the admin edge function with no retry on transient failures
violations.content:
`call` is the single entry point for every admin action against the `ADMIN_FN` edge function, and it issues one `fetch` with no retry. Edge functions are especially prone to transient failures — cold starts, worker recycling, and boot timeouts routinely produce `503`/`504` responses that succeed on an immediate retry. Today any such blip fails the user's admin action outright.

Unlike `get`, this is a `POST` that mutates state, so a blanket retry is not safe: an action that actually applied server-side but whose response was lost would be applied twice. Retries here should be limited to cases where the request provably did not reach the handler — a `fetch` rejection or a `503`/`504` — or the actions should be made idempotent (e.g. a client-generated request id the handler de-duplicates on) before retrying more broadly.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, add narrow retry logic to `call`. Retry only on conditions where the request almost certainly did not apply server-side: a `fetch` rejection before any response, or `res.status` of `503`/`504`. Do not retry on other `5xx`, on `4xx`, or on a well-formed response where `out.ok` is false, since the mutation may have partially applied. Use ~2 retries with exponential backoff (e.g. 300ms then 900ms) plus jitter. For stronger safety, generate a unique request id per `call` invocation, include it in the JSON body, and de-duplicate on it in the admin edge function handler so retries become fully idempotent; only widen the retry conditions once that de-duplication is in place. Preserve the existing error messages and return value.

violations.title: `loadBoard` aborts the whole board load if any one of eight independent queries fails
violations.content:
`loadBoard` fetches eight independent datasets (`v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, `games`, `sports_games`, `players`, `v_daily_losses`, `padel_sessions`) with `Promise.all`. A single rejection — a transient network error, a permissions issue on one view, or a missing/renamed table such as `padel_sessions` on a board that never plays padel — rejects the whole call, so the caller sees a total load failure and the UI renders nothing.

These sections are independent: card standings do not depend on padel sessions, and the daily-loss panel does not depend on the sports game log. The batch should report partial success so the sections that did load still render, with only the failed section showing an error or empty state.
violations.fixPrompt: In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, replace `Promise.all` with `Promise.allSettled` over the eight `get(...)` calls. Map each settled result to its `value` on fulfilment and to a safe empty default (`[]`) on rejection, and collect the rejection reasons into an `errors` field on the returned object (e.g. `{ standings, sportStandings, ..., errors }`) so callers can surface a per-section warning instead of failing the entire board render. Keep the existing `USE_MOCK` short-circuit and the returned property names unchanged so existing consumers keep working.
violations.snippet:
const [standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions] = await Promise.all([
    get(`v_standings?select=player_id,name,gp,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_sport_standings?select=sport,player_id,name,games,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&sport=neq.cards&order=name`),
    get(`v_padel_standings?select=player_id,name,archived,rounds,points_for,points_against&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`games?select=id,game_date,p1,p2,p3,p4,loser,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`sports_games?select=id,game_date,sport,a1,a2,b1,b2,score_a,score_b,points_target,session_id,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`players?select=id,name,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_daily_losses?select=player_id,name,losses&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&game_date=eq.${today}`),
    get(`padel_sessions?select=id,game_date,roster,courts,rounds,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=created_at.desc`),
  ]);
  return { standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions };

violations.title: `loadBoard` fetches unbounded `games` and `sports_games` history with no `limit`
violations.content:
The `games` and `sports_games` queries inside `loadBoard` specify `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc` but no `limit` or range header, so every call materializes the board's **entire** game history into an in-memory array. This collection has no size cap and grows monotonically for the life of the leaderboard.

The growth is amplified by how often it runs: `refresh()` calls `loadBoard()` and is invoked after every single write — every logged card game, every racquet game, and notably after *each individual match* in the Americano round-runner (`openSessionRunner` calls `await refresh(); draw();` on each `Log` tap). So a single padel night re-downloads and re-parses the full history dozens of times, each time larger than the last.

Downstream consumers hold the whole array too: `openGames()` builds `merged()` from all of `data.games` plus all of `data.sportsGames` and writes every row into `rows.innerHTML` in one shot, and `rowsHTML` calls `losingStreak(data?.games ?? [], p.player_id)` once per player over the full array. On a long-lived board viewed from a phone, the unbounded payload plus the unbounded DOM render is the realistic memory/latency failure point.

Add server-side pagination (a `limit` on the initial load, with an explicit "load more" for the history sheet) so the in-memory collection has a bounded size independent of how long the board has existed.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, bound the two history queries so the in-memory arrays cannot grow without limit. Add an explicit `limit` to the `games` and `sports_games` PostgREST queries (e.g. `&limit=200`), since both already sort newest-first via `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`. Introduce a named constant such as `HISTORY_LIMIT` at module scope rather than inlining the number.

Then make the truncation visible instead of silent: have `openGames()` in `js/app.js` render a "Load older games" affordance when the returned page is full (length === HISTORY_LIMIT), fetching the next page via a new paginated read helper that accepts an offset. Ensure the mock backend in `api.js` honours the same limit so demo mode matches production behaviour.

Also confirm that the aggregate views (`v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, `v_daily_losses`) are still the source of truth for all standings numbers, so limiting the raw game arrays cannot change any displayed ranking. The one place that consumes raw `data.games` for a computed value is `losingStreak` in `rowsHTML` — verify a truncated array still yields a correct streak, or cap the streak computation explicitly.

violations.title: `loadBoard` fetches unbounded `games` and `sports_games` history with no `limit`
violations.content:
The `games` and `sports_games` queries inside `loadBoard` specify `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc` but no `limit` or range header, so every call materializes the board's **entire** game history into an in-memory array. The growth is amplified by how often it runs: `refresh()` calls `loadBoard()` and is invoked after every single write — every logged card game, every racquet game, and notably after *each individual match* in the Americano round-runner (`openSessionRunner` calls `await refresh(); draw();` on each `Log` tap). [], p.player_id)` once per player over the full array. On a long-lived board viewed from a phone, the unbounded payload plus the unbounded DOM render is the realistic memory/latency failure point.

Add server-side pagination (a `limit` on the initial load, with an explicit "load more" for the history sheet) so the in-memory collection has a bounded size independent of how long the board has existed.

violations.title: `get` performs Supabase REST reads with no retry on transient failures
violations.content: `get` is the shared read primitive for every Supabase REST call in the app, but the single `fetch` has no retry wrapper. Any transient condition — a dropped connection, DNS blip, mobile network handoff, or a `502`/`503`/`429` from the Supabase edge — throws immediately and surfaces to the user as "Couldn't reach the server". Because this is a `GET` with no side effects, retrying is fully safe and idempotent, so this is the highest-value place to add backoff: a couple of retries would absorb the majority of these failures invisibly. The current code also collapses the distinction between retryable (`5xx`, `429`, network error) and non-retryable (`4xx`) responses.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, add retry-with-exponential-backoff to `get`. Wrap the `fetch` call in a loop of ~3 attempts. Retry when `fetch` itself rejects (network error) or when `res.status` is `429` or >= `500`; do not retry other `4xx` statuses — throw those immediately. Back off between attempts (e.g. 300ms, 600ms, 1200ms) with a small random jitter, and honour the `Retry-After` header if present on a `429`. After the final attempt, throw the existing `Couldn't reach the server (${res.status})` error so callers are unaffected. Consider extracting the retry loop into a small `fetchWithRetry` helper so it can be reused.

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Couldn't reach the server (${res.status})`);

violations.title: `call` invokes the admin edge function with no retry on transient failures
violations.content:
`call` is the single entry point for every admin action against the `ADMIN_FN` edge function, and it issues one `fetch` with no retry. Edge functions are especially prone to transient failures — cold starts, worker recycling, and boot timeouts routinely produce `503`/`504` responses that succeed on an immediate retry. Today any such blip fails the user's admin action outright.

Unlike `get`, this is a `POST` that mutates state, so a blanket retry is not safe: an action that actually applied server-side but whose response was lost would be applied twice. Retries here should be limited to cases where the request provably did not reach the handler — a `fetch` rejection or a `503`/`504` — or the actions should be made idempotent (e.g. a client-generated request id the handler de-duplicates on) before retrying more broadly.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, add narrow retry logic to `call`. Retry only on conditions where the request almost certainly did not apply server-side: a `fetch` rejection before any response, or `res.status` of `503`/`504`. Do not retry on other `5xx`, on `4xx`, or on a well-formed response where `out.ok` is false, since the mutation may have partially applied. Use ~2 retries with exponential backoff (e.g. 300ms then 900ms) plus jitter. For stronger safety, generate a unique request id per `call` invocation, include it in the JSON body, and de-duplicate on it in the admin edge function handler so retries become fully idempotent; only widen the retry conditions once that de-duplication is in place. Preserve the existing error messages and return value.

violations.title: `loadBoard` aborts the whole board load if any one of eight independent queries fails

A single rejection — a transient network error, a permissions issue on one view, or a missing/renamed table such as `padel_sessions` on a board that never plays padel — rejects the whole call, so the caller sees a total load failure and the UI renders nothing.

These sections are independent: card standings do not depend on padel sessions, and the daily-loss panel does not depend on the sports game log. The batch should report partial success so the sections that did load still render, with only the failed section showing an error or empty state.
violations.fixPrompt: In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, replace `Promise.all` with `Promise.allSettled` over the eight `get(...)` calls. Map each settled result to its `value` on fulfilment and to a safe empty default (`[]`) on rejection, and collect the rejection reasons into an `errors` field on the returned object (e.g. `{ standings, sportStandings, ..., errors }`) so callers can surface a per-section warning instead of failing the entire board render. Keep the existing `USE_MOCK` short-circuit and the returned property names unchanged so existing consumers keep working.

violations.title: Front end `app.js` has no client-side error reporting
violations.content:
`js/app.js` is the entire UI layer — it imports `./api.js`, `./export.mjs`, `./ranking.mjs`, and `./americano.mjs`, and drives the DOM directly (`document.createElement`, `box.querySelectorAll`, `r.addEventListener`). No error tracking SDK is imported here or in any sibling module, and there is no visible `globalThis.addEventListener('error', ...)` or `'unhandledrejection'` registration.

Every network call goes through `./api.js`, so a rejected fetch inside an event handler such as the `r.addEventListener` wiring becomes an unhandled rejection that the user sees only as a button that silently does nothing. Since this is a static client app with no server-rendered error page, there is no other channel through which such a failure could reach the maintainer.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, register global handlers early in module initialization: `globalThis.addEventListener('error', ...)` and `globalThis.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', ...)`, forwarding the error to an error tracking service. Gate initialization on a DSN value exported from `js/config.js` (and add the matching placeholder key to `js/config.example.js`) so that the mock/local mode driven by `USE_MOCK` does not report. As a minimum fallback if no external service is desired, surface these failures in the UI instead of letting them vanish.

violations.title: `rosterMem` is a module-level cache with no size limit or eviction policy
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a module-scoped object used as a cache of the last-used A/B roster split, keyed by `${boardId}:${sport}` and written on every successful racquet save (`rosterMem[memKey()] = { a: [...a], b: [...b] }` in the `save` handler of `openLogSport`). Entries are only ever added — nothing removes them, and there is no maximum entry count.

In practice the key space is bounded by (number of boards) × (5 sports), and each value holds at most four integer ids, so this will not realistically exhaust memory in a browser tab. It is flagged as a hygiene issue rather than a crash risk: the cache also never invalidates when a board is deleted via `openDeleteBoard`, so stale roster entries for deleted boards persist for the lifetime of the page.

A bounded structure with explicit eviction would make the growth characteristics obvious and drop entries for boards that no longer exist.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `js/app.js`, convert `rosterMem` from a bare object into a bounded LRU-style cache. Replace it with a `Map` (which preserves insertion order) and add a small helper that, on write, deletes the existing key before re-inserting it and then evicts the oldest entry while `size` exceeds a named constant such as `ROSTER_MEM_MAX` (a value like 20 is ample). Update the read in `restore()` and the write in the `save` handler of `openLogSport` to use `.get()`/`.set()` through that helper.

Additionally, clear entries for a deleted board: in `openDeleteBoard`, after the delete succeeds, remove every `rosterMem` key whose `boardId` prefix matches the deleted board so stale rosters do not survive the board itself.

const rosterMem = {};   // `${boardId}:${sport}` -> { a:[ids], b:[ids] }

violations.title: Module-level `data` cache is only refreshed on local writes, so remote changes and the date rollover never invalidate it
violations.content:
`data` (declared at line 49) holds the entire board payload — `standings`, `games`, `sportsGames`, `players`, `dailyLosses`, `padelSessions` — and is only repopulated by `loadBoard()` when `refresh()` or `switchBoard()` is called. Both are triggered exclusively by local user actions (initial `refresh()` at line 1221, a board switch, or a successful write from this tab). There is no TTL, no polling, no revalidation on `visibilitychange`/`focus`, and no realtime subscription to Supabase.

This is a shared leaderboard: several people log games from their own devices against the same `leaderboards` row. A tab left open shows stale standings indefinitely — every render path (`spotlightHTML`, `sportTablesHTML`, `padelTableHTML`, `padelSessionBanner`, `openGames`) reads from this snapshot.

The staleness is also time-based, not just write-based: `api.loadBoard()` resolves `localToday()` once at fetch time and filters `v_daily_losses` on `game_date=eq.<today>` (`js/api.js:179` and `js/api.js:187`). A tab open across midnight keeps rendering yesterday's row under the "Today's biggest loser" heading, while `padelSpotlightHTML` (line 1013) recomputes today's padel loser against a freshly-evaluated `api.localToday()` — so the two spotlights disagree about what "today" means.

The Americano round-runner is the worst case: `openSessionRunner` can stay open for a whole padel night while another phone logs rounds into the same `session_id`, and the live "tonight" standings silently omit them.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, add an invalidation strategy for the module-level `data` cache. At minimum: (1) record the fetch time alongside `data` in `loadBoard()`, and re-run `refresh()` on `document.visibilitychange` / `window.focus` when the snapshot is older than a short TTL (e.g. 30–60s); (2) also invalidate when `api.localToday()` no longer matches the date captured at fetch time, so the "Today's biggest loser" spotlight and `dailyLosses` do not survive a midnight rollover; (3) for `openSessionRunner`, poll `refresh()` + `draw()` on an interval (or subscribe to Supabase realtime on `sports_games`) while the runner sheet is open, clearing the interval in the sheet's close handler.

violations.title: `rosterMem` grows without bound and is never cleared when its board or players are removed
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a plain object cache keyed `${boardId}:${sport}` holding the last A/B roster split, written in `openLogSport`'s save handler (line 532) and read by `restore()` (lines 429–434). Nothing ever deletes an entry: not `openDeleteBoard` (which deletes the board and all its players), not `deletePlayer`/`restorePlayer`, not `switchBoard`.

`restore()` does filter out ids missing from `activePlayers()`, which prevents deleted players leaking into the picker, so the user-visible impact is limited. What remains is an entry-per-board-per-sport that accumulates for the lifetime of the page — including entries keyed to boards that no longer exist — and a subtle behavioural quirk: a player archived and later restored silently reappears pre-selected in the roster from a session logged before they were archived.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, invalidate `rosterMem` entries when their source data disappears: delete all keys starting with `${boardId}:` inside `openDeleteBoard`'s success branch, and drop the cached ids for a player in the `deletePlayer` handler in `openPlayers`. Alternatively store the roster memory with a timestamp and treat entries older than the current session (or older than a few hours) as expired inside `restore()`.

violations.title: Edge function `admin` has no error monitoring integration
violations.content:
The only import in this module is `https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2` — there is no Sentry, Bugsnag, Datadog, or OpenTelemetry SDK initialized. This is the sole server-side entry point of the application: it registers a handler via `Deno.serve` and fans out to database work (`Promise.all`), passcode verification (`crypto.subtle.digest`, `passcodeMatches`), and rate limiting (`fails.get`, `Date.now`). The visible error path consists only of the local `bad` and `json` helpers, which shape an HTTP response for the caller and report nothing outbound.

Because of that, a failure inside any handler branch — a Supabase query error, a malformed payload that slips past the `/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/` and `Number.isInteger` guards, or an unhandled promise rejection inside `Promise.all` — surfaces to the user as a status code and then disappears. Deno Deploy captures stderr, but nothing aggregates, alerts on, or de-duplicates these, so a regression affecting every write request looks identical to normal operation from the outside.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, add error monitoring around the `Deno.serve` handler. Wrap the top-level handler body in a try/catch that reports the caught error to an external service before returning the existing `bad(...)` response, and register a global `unhandledrejection` listener that reports as well. Use a Deno-compatible SDK (for example `https://esm.sh/@sentry/deno`) initialized from a `SENTRY_DSN` read via `Deno.env.get`, and skip initialization when the variable is absent so local runs are unaffected. Include the request path and the resolved action name as context on each report, but do not attach the passcode or any hashed credential material.

violations.title: HTTP handler `Deno.serve` has no response time or query duration instrumentation
violations.content:
The `Deno.serve` handler in this module is the application's only HTTP server, and no metrics library (`prom-client`, StatsD, OpenTelemetry) appears among its imports — the sole import is `https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2`. The visible call list shows `Date.now` used only for rate-limit bookkeeping alongside `fails.get`, not for timing.

As a result, request latency is unmeasured, and the Supabase queries this function issues — including the fan-out under `Promise.all` and the aggregate reads backing the standings views — have no recorded duration. A query that degrades as the games and sports games tables grow, or a slow `crypto.subtle.digest` path under load, will not be visible until requests start timing out.
violations.fixPrompt: Instrument the `Deno.serve` handler in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts` with timing: capture a start timestamp at the top of the handler, and on every exit path (including the `bad` error responses) record the elapsed duration together with the action name and response status. Also time the Supabase calls, especially the ones batched under `Promise.all`. Emit these either through an OpenTelemetry exporter or, if a full metrics backend is out of scope, as structured single-line records that Deno Deploy log ingestion can aggregate. Keep the instrumentation off the hot path when a metrics endpoint is not configured.

violations.title: Rate-limit map `fails` grows without bound and has no eviction
violations.content:
`fails` is a module-level `Map` keyed by client IP that acts as an in-memory cache for the brute-force lockout, but it has no size cap, no TTL sweep, and no eviction policy. An entry is added on every failed passcode attempt (`fails.set(ip, ...)`, line 124) and is only ever removed on a *successful* passcode (`fails.delete(ip)`, line 128). Entries whose `until` timestamp has already expired are never reclaimed — the lockout check at line 116 reads `rec.until > now` but leaves the stale record in place, so the map only grows for the lifetime of the Edge Function instance.

The key is derived from the `x-forwarded-for` header (line 113), which is request-controlled. Anyone who can reach the function can send POSTs with a wrong passcode and a fresh spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` value each time, inserting an unbounded number of distinct keys — and the per-IP lockout never engages, because every request lands on a brand-new key. Each entry is small, but with no upper bound the map grows linearly with request volume until the isolate hits its memory limit and the function crashes, taking down the only write path for the app.

Even without a malicious actor, ordinary traffic from many distinct client IPs (mobile networks rotate addresses) accumulates entries indefinitely, since only successfully-authenticated IPs are ever deleted.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, bound the in-memory `fails` map so it cannot grow without limit.

1. Add a `MAX_TRACKED = 10_000` (or similar) constant alongside `MAX_FAILS` and `LOCK_MS`.
2. Store a `seen: number` timestamp on each record so counters that never reached `MAX_FAILS` can be aged out.
3. Before inserting a new entry in the failure path (`fails.set(ip, ...)` near line 124), sweep expired records: iterate `fails` and `delete` any entry whose `until` is `0` or `<= now` and whose `seen` is older than `LOCK_MS`.
4. After the sweep, if `fails.size >= MAX_TRACKED`, evict the oldest entries (or clear the map) before adding the new one, so the map has a hard ceiling regardless of traffic.
5. Also `fails.delete(ip)` in the lockout check around line 116 when `rec.until <= now`, so expired lockouts are reclaimed on read as well.

Keep the existing behaviour otherwise: 5 wrong passcodes still triggers a 60s cooldown, and a correct passcode still clears the counter.
violations.snippet: const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>();

violations.title: Lockout counter in `fails` is never invalidated when its window expires
violations.content:
The in-memory `fails` map stores `{ n, until }` per IP, but the failure count `n` is only ever cleared on a *successful* passcode (`fails.delete(ip)` on line 128). When the lockout window at line 116 (`rec.until > now`) elapses, the stale `n` value survives — nothing resets it. On the next wrong passcode, line 123 computes `n = (rec?.n ?? 0) + 1`, which is already `>= MAX_FAILS`, so line 124 immediately re-locks the IP for another `LOCK_MS`.

The practical effect: once an IP crosses 5 failures, a single mistyped passcode at any later point — hours or days later — triggers a fresh 60s lockout, because the counter is stale cached state that never expires alongside the `until` timestamp it is paired with. The intended "5 wrong passcodes -> 60s cooldown" behaviour silently degrades into "1 wrong passcode -> 60s cooldown, forever" for that IP. For a shared-NAT friend group all hitting the same egress IP, one person's typo locks out everyone.

The fix is to treat an expired `until` as an invalidation signal and restart the count from zero.

violations.title: `fails` map has no eviction, so expired entries accumulate unboundedly
violations.content:
`const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>()` retains an entry per distinct client IP for the lifetime of the function instance. Entries are removed only on a successful passcode (line 128); an IP that fails once and never returns leaves its record in the map permanently. The `until` field encodes an expiry for the *lockout*, but nothing ever sweeps entries whose `until` has passed.

Each record is small, so this is not an immediate risk for a friend-group app on a warm instance, but the map is fed directly from the attacker-controlled `x-forwarded-for` header (line 113). A stream of requests with varied `X-Forwarded-For` values inserts an unbounded number of never-collected keys, and the retained stale entries are also what make the counter bug above persist indefinitely. A periodic or opportunistic sweep of records whose `until` has elapsed bounds the memory and gives the cached state a real expiry.
violations.snippet: const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>();

violations.title: `get` performs Supabase REST reads with no retry on transient failures
violations.content: `get` is the shared read primitive for every Supabase REST call in the app, but the single `fetch` has no retry wrapper. Any transient condition — a dropped connection, DNS blip, mobile network handoff, or a `502`/`503`/`429` from the Supabase edge — throws immediately and surfaces to the user as "Couldn't reach the server". Because this is a `GET` with no side effects, retrying is fully safe and idempotent, so this is the highest-value place to add backoff: a couple of retries would absorb the majority of these failures invisibly. The current code also collapses the distinction between retryable (`5xx`, `429`, network error) and non-retryable (`4xx`) responses.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, add retry-with-exponential-backoff to `get`. Wrap the `fetch` call in a loop of ~3 attempts. Retry when `fetch` itself rejects (network error) or when `res.status` is `429` or >= `500`; do not retry other `4xx` statuses — throw those immediately. Back off between attempts (e.g. 300ms, 600ms, 1200ms) with a small random jitter, and honour the `Retry-After` header if present on a `429`. After the final attempt, throw the existing `Couldn't reach the server (${res.status})` error so callers are unaffected. Consider extracting the retry loop into a small `fetchWithRetry` helper so it can be reused.
violations.snippet:
const res = await fetch(`${SUPABASE_URL}/rest/v1/${path}`, { headers: H });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Couldn't reach the server (${res.status})`);

violations.title: `call` invokes the admin edge function with no retry on transient failures
violations.content:
`call` is the single entry point for every admin action against the `ADMIN_FN` edge function, and it issues one `fetch` with no retry. Edge functions are especially prone to transient failures — cold starts, worker recycling, and boot timeouts routinely produce `503`/`504` responses that succeed on an immediate retry. Today any such blip fails the user's admin action outright.

Unlike `get`, this is a `POST` that mutates state, so a blanket retry is not safe: an action that actually applied server-side but whose response was lost would be applied twice. Retries here should be limited to cases where the request provably did not reach the handler — a `fetch` rejection or a `503`/`504` — or the actions should be made idempotent (e.g. a client-generated request id the handler de-duplicates on) before retrying more broadly.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, add narrow retry logic to `call`. Retry only on conditions where the request almost certainly did not apply server-side: a `fetch` rejection before any response, or `res.status` of `503`/`504`. Do not retry on other `5xx`, on `4xx`, or on a well-formed response where `out.ok` is false, since the mutation may have partially applied. Use ~2 retries with exponential backoff (e.g. 300ms then 900ms) plus jitter. For stronger safety, generate a unique request id per `call` invocation, include it in the JSON body, and de-duplicate on it in the admin edge function handler so retries become fully idempotent; only widen the retry conditions once that de-duplication is in place. Preserve the existing error messages and return value.

violations.title: `loadBoard` aborts the whole board load if any one of eight independent queries fails
violations.content:
`loadBoard` fetches eight independent datasets (`v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, `games`, `sports_games`, `players`, `v_daily_losses`, `padel_sessions`) with `Promise.all`. A single rejection — a transient network error, a permissions issue on one view, or a missing/renamed table such as `padel_sessions` on a board that never plays padel — rejects the whole call, so the caller sees a total load failure and the UI renders nothing.

These sections are independent: card standings do not depend on padel sessions, and the daily-loss panel does not depend on the sports game log. The batch should report partial success so the sections that did load still render, with only the failed section showing an error or empty state.
violations.fixPrompt: In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, replace `Promise.all` with `Promise.allSettled` over the eight `get(...)` calls. Map each settled result to its `value` on fulfilment and to a safe empty default (`[]`) on rejection, and collect the rejection reasons into an `errors` field on the returned object (e.g. `{ standings, sportStandings, ..., errors }`) so callers can surface a per-section warning instead of failing the entire board render. Keep the existing `USE_MOCK` short-circuit and the returned property names unchanged so existing consumers keep working.
violations.snippet:
const [standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions] = await Promise.all([
    get(`v_standings?select=player_id,name,gp,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_sport_standings?select=sport,player_id,name,games,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&sport=neq.cards&order=name`),
    get(`v_padel_standings?select=player_id,name,archived,rounds,points_for,points_against&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`games?select=id,game_date,p1,p2,p3,p4,loser,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`sports_games?select=id,game_date,sport,a1,a2,b1,b2,score_a,score_b,points_target,session_id,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`players?select=id,name,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_daily_losses?select=player_id,name,losses&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&game_date=eq.${today}`),
    get(`padel_sessions?select=id,game_date,roster,courts,rounds,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=created_at.desc`),
  ]);
  return { standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions };

violations.title: `loadBoard` fetches unbounded `games` and `sports_games` history with no `limit`
violations.content:
The `games` and `sports_games` queries inside `loadBoard` specify `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc` but no `limit` or range header, so every call materializes the board's **entire** game history into an in-memory array. This collection has no size cap and grows monotonically for the life of the leaderboard.

The growth is amplified by how often it runs: `refresh()` calls `loadBoard()` and is invoked after every single write — every logged card game, every racquet game, and notably after *each individual match* in the Americano round-runner (`openSessionRunner` calls `await refresh(); draw();` on each `Log` tap). So a single padel night re-downloads and re-parses the full history dozens of times, each time larger than the last.

Downstream consumers hold the whole array too: `openGames()` builds `merged()` from all of `data.games` plus all of `data.sportsGames` and writes every row into `rows.innerHTML` in one shot, and `rowsHTML` calls `losingStreak(data?.games ?? [], p.player_id)` once per player over the full array. On a long-lived board viewed from a phone, the unbounded payload plus the unbounded DOM render is the realistic memory/latency failure point.

Add server-side pagination (a `limit` on the initial load, with an explicit "load more" for the history sheet) so the in-memory collection has a bounded size independent of how long the board has existed.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, bound the two history queries so the in-memory arrays cannot grow without limit. Add an explicit `limit` to the `games` and `sports_games` PostgREST queries (e.g. `&limit=200`), since both already sort newest-first via `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`. Introduce a named constant such as `HISTORY_LIMIT` at module scope rather than inlining the number.

Then make the truncation visible instead of silent: have `openGames()` in `js/app.js` render a "Load older games" affordance when the returned page is full (length === HISTORY_LIMIT), fetching the next page via a new paginated read helper that accepts an offset. Ensure the mock backend in `api.js` honours the same limit so demo mode matches production behaviour.

Also confirm that the aggregate views (`v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, `v_daily_losses`) are still the source of truth for all standings numbers, so limiting the raw game arrays cannot change any displayed ranking. The one place that consumes raw `data.games` for a computed value is `losingStreak` in `rowsHTML` — verify a truncated array still yields a correct streak, or cap the streak computation explicitly.

violations.title: Front end `app.js` has no client-side error reporting
violations.content:
`js/app.js` is the entire UI layer — it imports `./api.js`, `./export.mjs`, `./ranking.mjs`, and `./americano.mjs`, and drives the DOM directly (`document.createElement`, `box.querySelectorAll`, `r.addEventListener`). No error tracking SDK is imported here or in any sibling module, and there is no visible `globalThis.addEventListener('error', ...)` or `'unhandledrejection'` registration.

Every network call goes through `./api.js`, so a rejected fetch inside an event handler such as the `r.addEventListener` wiring becomes an unhandled rejection that the user sees only as a button that silently does nothing. Since this is a static client app with no server-rendered error page, there is no other channel through which such a failure could reach the maintainer.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, register global handlers early in module initialization: `globalThis.addEventListener('error', ...)` and `globalThis.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', ...)`, forwarding the error to an error tracking service. Gate initialization on a DSN value exported from `js/config.js` (and add the matching placeholder key to `js/config.example.js`) so that the mock/local mode driven by `USE_MOCK` does not report. As a minimum fallback if no external service is desired, surface these failures in the UI instead of letting them vanish.
violations.snippet: import * as api from './api.js';

violations.title: `rosterMem` is a module-level cache with no size limit or eviction policy
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a module-scoped object used as a cache of the last-used A/B roster split, keyed by `${boardId}:${sport}` and written on every successful racquet save (`rosterMem[memKey()] = { a: [...a], b: [...b] }` in the `save` handler of `openLogSport`). Entries are only ever added — nothing removes them, and there is no maximum entry count.

In practice the key space is bounded by (number of boards) × (5 sports), and each value holds at most four integer ids, so this will not realistically exhaust memory in a browser tab. It is flagged as a hygiene issue rather than a crash risk: the cache also never invalidates when a board is deleted via `openDeleteBoard`, so stale roster entries for deleted boards persist for the lifetime of the page.

A bounded structure with explicit eviction would make the growth characteristics obvious and drop entries for boards that no longer exist.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `js/app.js`, convert `rosterMem` from a bare object into a bounded LRU-style cache. Replace it with a `Map` (which preserves insertion order) and add a small helper that, on write, deletes the existing key before re-inserting it and then evicts the oldest entry while `size` exceeds a named constant such as `ROSTER_MEM_MAX` (a value like 20 is ample). Update the read in `restore()` and the write in the `save` handler of `openLogSport` to use `.get()`/`.set()` through that helper.

Additionally, clear entries for a deleted board: in `openDeleteBoard`, after the delete succeeds, remove every `rosterMem` key whose `boardId` prefix matches the deleted board so stale rosters do not survive the board itself.
violations.snippet:
let lastSport = 'tt_singles';
const rosterMem = {};   // `${boardId}:${sport}` -> { a:[ids], b:[ids] }

violations.title: Module-level `data` cache is only refreshed on local writes, so remote changes and the date rollover never invalidate it
violations.content:
`data` (declared at line 49) holds the entire board payload — `standings`, `games`, `sportsGames`, `players`, `dailyLosses`, `padelSessions` — and is only repopulated by `loadBoard()` when `refresh()` or `switchBoard()` is called. Both are triggered exclusively by local user actions (initial `refresh()` at line 1221, a board switch, or a successful write from this tab). There is no TTL, no polling, no revalidation on `visibilitychange`/`focus`, and no realtime subscription to Supabase.

This is a shared leaderboard: several people log games from their own devices against the same `leaderboards` row. A tab left open shows stale standings indefinitely — every render path (`spotlightHTML`, `sportTablesHTML`, `padelTableHTML`, `padelSessionBanner`, `openGames`) reads from this snapshot.

The staleness is also time-based, not just write-based: `api.loadBoard()` resolves `localToday()` once at fetch time and filters `v_daily_losses` on `game_date=eq.<today>` (`js/api.js:179` and `js/api.js:187`). A tab open across midnight keeps rendering yesterday's row under the "Today's biggest loser" heading, while `padelSpotlightHTML` (line 1013) recomputes today's padel loser against a freshly-evaluated `api.localToday()` — so the two spotlights disagree about what "today" means.

The Americano round-runner is the worst case: `openSessionRunner` can stay open for a whole padel night while another phone logs rounds into the same `session_id`, and the live "tonight" standings silently omit them.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, add an invalidation strategy for the module-level `data` cache. At minimum: (1) record the fetch time alongside `data` in `loadBoard()`, and re-run `refresh()` on `document.visibilitychange` / `window.focus` when the snapshot is older than a short TTL (e.g. 30–60s); (2) also invalidate when `api.localToday()` no longer matches the date captured at fetch time, so the "Today's biggest loser" spotlight and `dailyLosses` do not survive a midnight rollover; (3) for `openSessionRunner`, poll `refresh()` + `draw()` on an interval (or subscribe to Supabase realtime on `sports_games`) while the runner sheet is open, clearing the interval in the sheet's close handler.

violations.title: `rosterMem` grows without bound and is never cleared when its board or players are removed
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a plain object cache keyed `${boardId}:${sport}` holding the last A/B roster split, written in `openLogSport`'s save handler (line 532) and read by `restore()` (lines 429–434). Nothing ever deletes an entry: not `openDeleteBoard` (which deletes the board and all its players), not `deletePlayer`/`restorePlayer`, not `switchBoard`.

`restore()` does filter out ids missing from `activePlayers()`, which prevents deleted players leaking into the picker, so the user-visible impact is limited. What remains is an entry-per-board-per-sport that accumulates for the lifetime of the page — including entries keyed to boards that no longer exist — and a subtle behavioural quirk: a player archived and later restored silently reappears pre-selected in the roster from a session logged before they were archived.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, invalidate `rosterMem` entries when their source data disappears: delete all keys starting with `${boardId}:` inside `openDeleteBoard`'s success branch, and drop the cached ids for a player in the `deletePlayer` handler in `openPlayers`. Alternatively store the roster memory with a timestamp and treat entries older than the current session (or older than a few hours) as expired inside `restore()`.
violations.snippet:
let lastSport = 'tt_singles';
const rosterMem = {};   // `${boardId}:${sport}` -> { a:[ids], b:[ids] }

violations.title: Edge function `admin` has no error monitoring integration
violations.content:
The only import in this module is `https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2` — there is no Sentry, Bugsnag, Datadog, or OpenTelemetry SDK initialized. This is the sole server-side entry point of the application: it registers a handler via `Deno.serve` and fans out to database work (`Promise.all`), passcode verification (`crypto.subtle.digest`, `passcodeMatches`), and rate limiting (`fails.get`, `Date.now`). The visible error path consists only of the local `bad` and `json` helpers, which shape an HTTP response for the caller and report nothing outbound.

Because of that, a failure inside any handler branch — a Supabase query error, a malformed payload that slips past the `/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/` and `Number.isInteger` guards, or an unhandled promise rejection inside `Promise.all` — surfaces to the user as a status code and then disappears. Deno Deploy captures stderr, but nothing aggregates, alerts on, or de-duplicates these, so a regression affecting every write request looks identical to normal operation from the outside.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, add error monitoring around the `Deno.serve` handler. Wrap the top-level handler body in a try/catch that reports the caught error to an external service before returning the existing `bad(...)` response, and register a global `unhandledrejection` listener that reports as well. Use a Deno-compatible SDK (for example `https://esm.sh/@sentry/deno`) initialized from a `SENTRY_DSN` read via `Deno.env.get`, and skip initialization when the variable is absent so local runs are unaffected. Include the request path and the resolved action name as context on each report, but do not attach the passcode or any hashed credential material.
violations.snippet: // LOTD admin Edge Function (v3) — the ONLY write path.

violations.title: HTTP handler `Deno.serve` has no response time or query duration instrumentation
violations.content:
The `Deno.serve` handler in this module is the application's only HTTP server, and no metrics library (`prom-client`, StatsD, OpenTelemetry) appears among its imports — the sole import is `https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2`. The visible call list shows `Date.now` used only for rate-limit bookkeeping alongside `fails.get`, not for timing.

As a result, request latency is unmeasured, and the Supabase queries this function issues — including the fan-out under `Promise.all` and the aggregate reads backing the standings views — have no recorded duration. A query that degrades as the games and sports games tables grow, or a slow `crypto.subtle.digest` path under load, will not be visible until requests start timing out.
violations.fixPrompt: Instrument the `Deno.serve` handler in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts` with timing: capture a start timestamp at the top of the handler, and on every exit path (including the `bad` error responses) record the elapsed duration together with the action name and response status. Also time the Supabase calls, especially the ones batched under `Promise.all`. Emit these either through an OpenTelemetry exporter or, if a full metrics backend is out of scope, as structured single-line records that Deno Deploy log ingestion can aggregate. Keep the instrumentation off the hot path when a metrics endpoint is not configured.
violations.snippet: // LOTD admin Edge Function (v3) — the ONLY write path.

violations.title: Rate-limit map `fails` grows without bound and has no eviction
violations.content:
`fails` is a module-level `Map` keyed by client IP that acts as an in-memory cache for the brute-force lockout, but it has no size cap, no TTL sweep, and no eviction policy. An entry is added on every failed passcode attempt (`fails.set(ip, ...)`, line 124) and is only ever removed on a *successful* passcode (`fails.delete(ip)`, line 128). Entries whose `until` timestamp has already expired are never reclaimed — the lockout check at line 116 reads `rec.until > now` but leaves the stale record in place, so the map only grows for the lifetime of the Edge Function instance.

The key is derived from the `x-forwarded-for` header (line 113), which is request-controlled. Anyone who can reach the function can send POSTs with a wrong passcode and a fresh spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` value each time, inserting an unbounded number of distinct keys — and the per-IP lockout never engages, because every request lands on a brand-new key. Each entry is small, but with no upper bound the map grows linearly with request volume until the isolate hits its memory limit and the function crashes, taking down the only write path for the app.

Even without a malicious actor, ordinary traffic from many distinct client IPs (mobile networks rotate addresses) accumulates entries indefinitely, since only successfully-authenticated IPs are ever deleted.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, bound the in-memory `fails` map so it cannot grow without limit.

1. Add a `MAX_TRACKED = 10_000` (or similar) constant alongside `MAX_FAILS` and `LOCK_MS`.
2. Store a `seen: number` timestamp on each record so counters that never reached `MAX_FAILS` can be aged out.
3. Before inserting a new entry in the failure path (`fails.set(ip, ...)` near line 124), sweep expired records: iterate `fails` and `delete` any entry whose `until` is `0` or `<= now` and whose `seen` is older than `LOCK_MS`.
4. After the sweep, if `fails.size >= MAX_TRACKED`, evict the oldest entries (or clear the map) before adding the new one, so the map has a hard ceiling regardless of traffic.
5. Also `fails.delete(ip)` in the lockout check around line 116 when `rec.until <= now`, so expired lockouts are reclaimed on read as well.

Keep the existing behaviour otherwise: 5 wrong passcodes still triggers a 60s cooldown, and a correct passcode still clears the counter.
violations.snippet: const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>();

violations.title: Lockout counter in `fails` is never invalidated when its window expires
violations.content:
The in-memory `fails` map stores `{ n, until }` per IP, but the failure count `n` is only ever cleared on a *successful* passcode (`fails.delete(ip)` on line 128). When the lockout window at line 116 (`rec.until > now`) elapses, the stale `n` value survives — nothing resets it. On the next wrong passcode, line 123 computes `n = (rec?.n ?? 0) + 1`, which is already `>= MAX_FAILS`, so line 124 immediately re-locks the IP for another `LOCK_MS`.

The practical effect: once an IP crosses 5 failures, a single mistyped passcode at any later point — hours or days later — triggers a fresh 60s lockout, because the counter is stale cached state that never expires alongside the `until` timestamp it is paired with. The intended "5 wrong passcodes -> 60s cooldown" behaviour silently degrades into "1 wrong passcode -> 60s cooldown, forever" for that IP. For a shared-NAT friend group all hitting the same egress IP, one person's typo locks out everyone.

The fix is to treat an expired `until` as an invalidation signal and restart the count from zero.

violations.title: `fails` map has no eviction, so expired entries accumulate unboundedly
violations.content:
`const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>()` retains an entry per distinct client IP for the lifetime of the function instance. Entries are removed only on a successful passcode (line 128); an IP that fails once and never returns leaves its record in the map permanently. The `until` field encodes an expiry for the *lockout*, but nothing ever sweeps entries whose `until` has passed.

Each record is small, so this is not an immediate risk for a friend-group app on a warm instance, but the map is fed directly from the attacker-controlled `x-forwarded-for` header (line 113). A stream of requests with varied `X-Forwarded-For` values inserts an unbounded number of never-collected keys, and the retained stale entries are also what make the counter bug above persist indefinitely. A periodic or opportunistic sweep of records whose `until` has elapsed bounds the memory and gives the cached state a real expiry.
violations.snippet: const fails = new Map<string, { n: number; until: number }>();

violations.title: `loadBoard` fetches unbounded `games` and `sports_games` history with no `limit`
violations.content:
The `games` and `sports_games` queries inside `loadBoard` specify `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc` but no `limit` or range header, so every call materializes the board's **entire** game history into an in-memory array. This collection has no size cap and grows monotonically for the life of the leaderboard.

The growth is amplified by how often it runs: `refresh()` calls `loadBoard()` and is invoked after every single write — every logged card game, every racquet game, and notably after *each individual match* in the Americano round-runner (`openSessionRunner` calls `await refresh(); draw();` on each `Log` tap). So a single padel night re-downloads and re-parses the full history dozens of times, each time larger than the last.

Downstream consumers hold the whole array too: `openGames()` builds `merged()` from all of `data.games` plus all of `data.sportsGames` and writes every row into `rows.innerHTML` in one shot, and `rowsHTML` calls `losingStreak(data?.games ?? [], p.player_id)` once per player over the full array. On a long-lived board viewed from a phone, the unbounded payload plus the unbounded DOM render is the realistic memory/latency failure point.

Add server-side pagination (a `limit` on the initial load, with an explicit "load more" for the history sheet) so the in-memory collection has a bounded size independent of how long the board has existed.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `loadBoard` in `js/api.js`, bound the two history queries so the in-memory arrays cannot grow without limit. Add an explicit `limit` to the `games` and `sports_games` PostgREST queries (e.g. `&limit=200`), since both already sort newest-first via `order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`. Introduce a named constant such as `HISTORY_LIMIT` at module scope rather than inlining the number.

Then make the truncation visible instead of silent: have `openGames()` in `js/app.js` render a "Load older games" affordance when the returned page is full (length === HISTORY_LIMIT), fetching the next page via a new paginated read helper that accepts an offset. Ensure the mock backend in `api.js` honours the same limit so demo mode matches production behaviour.

Also confirm that the aggregate views (`v_standings`, `v_sport_standings`, `v_padel_standings`, `v_daily_losses`) are still the source of truth for all standings numbers, so limiting the raw game arrays cannot change any displayed ranking. The one place that consumes raw `data.games` for a computed value is `losingStreak` in `rowsHTML` — verify a truncated array still yields a correct streak, or cap the streak computation explicitly.

violations.title: Front end `app.js` has no client-side error reporting
violations.content:
`js/app.js` is the entire UI layer — it imports `./api.js`, `./export.mjs`, `./ranking.mjs`, and `./americano.mjs`, and drives the DOM directly (`document.createElement`, `box.querySelectorAll`, `r.addEventListener`). No error tracking SDK is imported here or in any sibling module, and there is no visible `globalThis.addEventListener('error', ...)` or `'unhandledrejection'` registration.

Every network call goes through `./api.js`, so a rejected fetch inside an event handler such as the `r.addEventListener` wiring becomes an unhandled rejection that the user sees only as a button that silently does nothing. Since this is a static client app with no server-rendered error page, there is no other channel through which such a failure could reach the maintainer.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, register global handlers early in module initialization: `globalThis.addEventListener('error', ...)` and `globalThis.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', ...)`, forwarding the error to an error tracking service. Gate initialization on a DSN value exported from `js/config.js` (and add the matching placeholder key to `js/config.example.js`) so that the mock/local mode driven by `USE_MOCK` does not report. As a minimum fallback if no external service is desired, surface these failures in the UI instead of letting them vanish.
violations.snippet: import * as api from './api.js';

violations.title: `rosterMem` is a module-level cache with no size limit or eviction policy
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a module-scoped object used as a cache of the last-used A/B roster split, keyed by `${boardId}:${sport}` and written on every successful racquet save (`rosterMem[memKey()] = { a: [...a], b: [...b] }` in the `save` handler of `openLogSport`). Entries are only ever added — nothing removes them, and there is no maximum entry count.

In practice the key space is bounded by (number of boards) × (5 sports), and each value holds at most four integer ids, so this will not realistically exhaust memory in a browser tab. It is flagged as a hygiene issue rather than a crash risk: the cache also never invalidates when a board is deleted via `openDeleteBoard`, so stale roster entries for deleted boards persist for the lifetime of the page.

A bounded structure with explicit eviction would make the growth characteristics obvious and drop entries for boards that no longer exist.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `js/app.js`, convert `rosterMem` from a bare object into a bounded LRU-style cache. Replace it with a `Map` (which preserves insertion order) and add a small helper that, on write, deletes the existing key before re-inserting it and then evicts the oldest entry while `size` exceeds a named constant such as `ROSTER_MEM_MAX` (a value like 20 is ample). Update the read in `restore()` and the write in the `save` handler of `openLogSport` to use `.get()`/`.set()` through that helper.

Additionally, clear entries for a deleted board: in `openDeleteBoard`, after the delete succeeds, remove every `rosterMem` key whose `boardId` prefix matches the deleted board so stale rosters do not survive the board itself.
violations.snippet:
let lastSport = 'tt_singles';
const rosterMem = {};   // `${boardId}:${sport}` -> { a:[ids], b:[ids] }

violations.title: Module-level `data` cache is only refreshed on local writes, so remote changes and the date rollover never invalidate it
violations.content:
`data` (declared at line 49) holds the entire board payload — `standings`, `games`, `sportsGames`, `players`, `dailyLosses`, `padelSessions` — and is only repopulated by `loadBoard()` when `refresh()` or `switchBoard()` is called. Both are triggered exclusively by local user actions (initial `refresh()` at line 1221, a board switch, or a successful write from this tab). There is no TTL, no polling, no revalidation on `visibilitychange`/`focus`, and no realtime subscription to Supabase.

This is a shared leaderboard: several people log games from their own devices against the same `leaderboards` row. A tab left open shows stale standings indefinitely — every render path (`spotlightHTML`, `sportTablesHTML`, `padelTableHTML`, `padelSessionBanner`, `openGames`) reads from this snapshot.

The staleness is also time-based, not just write-based: `api.loadBoard()` resolves `localToday()` once at fetch time and filters `v_daily_losses` on `game_date=eq.<today>` (`js/api.js:179` and `js/api.js:187`). A tab open across midnight keeps rendering yesterday's row under the "Today's biggest loser" heading, while `padelSpotlightHTML` (line 1013) recomputes today's padel loser against a freshly-evaluated `api.localToday()` — so the two spotlights disagree about what "today" means.

The Americano round-runner is the worst case: `openSessionRunner` can stay open for a whole padel night while another phone logs rounds into the same `session_id`, and the live "tonight" standings silently omit them.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, add an invalidation strategy for the module-level `data` cache. At minimum: (1) record the fetch time alongside `data` in `loadBoard()`, and re-run `refresh()` on `document.visibilitychange` / `window.focus` when the snapshot is older than a short TTL (e.g. 30–60s); (2) also invalidate when `api.localToday()` no longer matches the date captured at fetch time, so the "Today's biggest loser" spotlight and `dailyLosses` do not survive a midnight rollover; (3) for `openSessionRunner`, poll `refresh()` + `draw()` on an interval (or subscribe to Supabase realtime on `sports_games`) while the runner sheet is open, clearing the interval in the sheet's close handler.

violations.title: `rosterMem` grows without bound and is never cleared when its board or players are removed
violations.content:
`rosterMem` is a plain object cache keyed `${boardId}:${sport}` holding the last A/B roster split, written in `openLogSport`'s save handler (line 532) and read by `restore()` (lines 429–434). Nothing ever deletes an entry: not `openDeleteBoard` (which deletes the board and all its players), not `deletePlayer`/`restorePlayer`, not `switchBoard`.

`restore()` does filter out ids missing from `activePlayers()`, which prevents deleted players leaking into the picker, so the user-visible impact is limited. What remains is an entry-per-board-per-sport that accumulates for the lifetime of the page — including entries keyed to boards that no longer exist — and a subtle behavioural quirk: a player archived and later restored silently reappears pre-selected in the roster from a session logged before they were archived.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, invalidate `rosterMem` entries when their source data disappears: delete all keys starting with `${boardId}:` inside `openDeleteBoard`'s success branch, and drop the cached ids for a player in the `deletePlayer` handler in `openPlayers`. Alternatively store the roster memory with a timestamp and treat entries older than the current session (or older than a few hours) as expired inside `restore()`.
