violations.title: Wildcard CORS origin fails open when `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` is unset
violations.content:
`corsHeaders` falls back to `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: '*'` whenever the `ALLOWED` list is empty (line 39), and `ALLOWED` is derived from the optional `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` env var via `?? ''` (line 17). This is a fail-open default: if `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` is never set, is cleared, or is set to a value that filters down to an empty list (e.g. only whitespace or commas), the function silently begins accepting cross-origin browser requests from **any** site — with no deploy-time error and no log line to signal the misconfiguration.

This matters more than usual here because this function is, per its own header comment, "the ONLY write path" and it runs with the `service_role` key, which bypasses RLS. The preflight also explicitly allows the `authorization` and `apikey` headers (line 32), so an arbitrary origin is permitted to send them.

The practical exploitability is limited — `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is never set, so browsers will not attach cookies, and every action is still gated behind `passcodeMatches`. So this is a defence-in-depth / deployment-safety problem rather than a direct authentication bypass. Still, the origin allowlist is the intended second layer, and a fallback that quietly disables it based on a missing env var is the wrong default for the production write path. The dev-convenience case should be opted into explicitly rather than inferred from absence of config.
violations.fixPrompt:
In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the permissive CORS fallback explicit instead of inferred from a missing env var.

1. Add a dedicated dev flag, e.g. `const DEV_OPEN_CORS = Deno.env.get('DEV_OPEN_CORS') === 'true';`
2. In `corsHeaders`, only emit `h['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = '*'` when `DEV_OPEN_CORS` is true. Otherwise, set the header only when `ALLOWED.includes(origin)` — omitting it entirely for non-matching origins, as the current `else if` branch already does correctly.
3. At module load, if `ALLOWED.length === 0 && !DEV_OPEN_CORS`, emit a clear startup warning via `console.warn` (or throw) so a missing/empty `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` is loud rather than silent.

Keep the existing `Vary: Origin` header and the `authorization, apikey, content-type` allow-headers list unchanged.

violations.title: `call` swallows the JSON parse failure and reports a misleading `Request failed (200)`
violations.content: `res.json().catch(() => ({}))` discards the parse error and substitutes `{}`. For a successful HTTP response with an unparseable or empty body (proxy-truncated response, HTML error page from an edge failure, 204), `out.ok` is `undefined`, so line 213 throws `Request failed (200)` — an error message that contradicts itself and describes a failure mode that did not occur. The real cause (the body was not JSON) is completely lost, and the same message is produced for network-level and body-level problems alike.
violations.fixPrompt: In `call` in `js/api.js`, capture the parse failure distinctly, e.g. `let out; try { out = await res.json(); } catch (e) { throw new Error(res.ok ? `Server sent an unreadable response (${res.status})` : `Request failed (${res.status})`, { cause: e }); }` and only then check `!res.ok || !out.ok`.
violations.snippet:
const out = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
  if (!res.ok || !out.ok) throw new Error(out.error || `Request failed (${res.status})`);

violations.title: `loadBoard` uses `Promise.all`, so one failing query blanks the entire board
violations.content:
`loadBoard` fans out eight independent REST queries through `Promise.all`. `get` throws on any non-OK response (line 164), and `Promise.all` rejects on the first rejection, so a single failing or missing resource — for example the `padel_sessions` table or the `v_padel_standings` view returning 404/500 on a board that does not even play padel — discards the seven successful responses. The caller in `js/app.js:134-138` catches this and sets `error`, leaving the user with no standings, no games and no player list instead of a board that is merely missing its padel panel.

This is the failure mode where one unrelated query brings down every feature on the screen; the data is naturally partitionable and should degrade per-section.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, change `loadBoard` to use `Promise.allSettled` and map each result to its value or a safe empty fallback (`[]`), so a failure in one query does not discard the others. Keep hard-failing only for the queries the board cannot render without (e.g. `players` and `standings`), and return a per-section error marker for the rest so `js/app.js` can render a partial board with an inline notice instead of an empty screen.
violations.snippet:
const [standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions] = await Promise.all([
    get(`v_standings?select=player_id,name,gp,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_sport_standings?select=sport,player_id,name,games,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&sport=neq.cards&order=name`),
    get(`v_padel_standings?select=player_id,name,archived,rounds,points_for,points_against&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`games?select=id,game_date,p1,p2,p3,p4,loser,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`sports_games?select=id,game_date,sport,a1,a2,b1,b2,score_a,score_b,points_target,session_id,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`players?select=id,name,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_daily_losses?select=player_id,name,losses&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&game_date=eq.${today}`),
    get(`padel_sessions?select=id,game_date,roster,courts,rounds,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=created_at.desc`),
  ]);
  return { standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions };

violations.title: `listLeaderboards` returns a raw array in mock mode but a Promise otherwise
violations.content: `listLeaderboards` is declared as a plain arrow function whose two branches return different kinds of value: when `USE_MOCK` is true it returns the synchronous array produced by `mock.listLeaderboards()`, and otherwise it returns the Promise returned by `get(...)`. The return type is therefore `Array | Promise<Array>` depending on a module-level flag. It happens to work today only because every caller (`loadBoards` in `js/app.js`) awaits the result, and `await` on a non-thenable is a no-op. Any caller that treats the result synchronously (or that chains `.then`/`.catch` on it) would break in exactly one of the two modes, and the mock branch silently swallows the possibility of rejection handling. The same shape is repeated in every exported wrapper in this file.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, make the mock and live branches return the same wrapped type. Either declare `listLeaderboards` as `async` (so the mock branch is auto-wrapped in a Promise), or wrap the mock branch explicitly with `Promise.resolve(...)`. Apply the same treatment to the other exported wrappers (`createLeaderboard`, `renameLeaderboard`, `deleteLeaderboard`, `addPlayer`, `deletePlayer`, `restorePlayer`, `logGame`, `undoLast`, `editLoser`, `deleteGame`, `logSportsGame`, `createPadelSession`, `undoLastSports`, `editSportsScore`, `deleteSportsGame`) so every export consistently returns a Promise.
violations.snippet:
export const listLeaderboards = () =>
  USE_MOCK ? mock.listLeaderboards() : get('leaderboards?select=id,name,game_types,points_target&order=name');

violations.title: `logSportsGame` returns either a plain object or a Promise depending on `USE_MOCK`
violations.content: `logSportsGame` explicitly returns the result of a ternary whose branches have different types: `mock.logSportsGame(...)` returns the newly created game object synchronously, while `call('log_sports_game', ...)` returns a Promise resolving to the server row. Callers such as the `save` handler in `openLogSport` and the round-runner's log handler in `js/app.js` pass this through `attempt(...)`, which awaits it — so failures in the mock branch would throw synchronously at call time rather than rejecting, and error handling differs between the two modes. A function that sometimes returns a wrapped value and sometimes the raw value is easy to misuse as the codebase grows.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, mark `logSportsGame` as `async` (or wrap the mock branch in `Promise.resolve(...)`) so both branches return a Promise resolving to the created sports-game row, regardless of `USE_MOCK`.

violations.title: Mock `renameLeaderboard` returns `undefined` when the board id is unknown
violations.content: `renameLeaderboard` in the mock backend does `const b = board(id); if (b) { ... } return b;` — so when `board(id)` finds no matching board it returns `undefined`, while the success path returns the mutated board object and the live path (`call('rename_leaderboard', ...)`) resolves to a server row. The caller in `openRenameBoard` (`js/app.js`) treats any non-throwing result as success, so a rename against a stale or deleted `boardId` in mock mode silently reports success and closes the sheet even though nothing was renamed. Mixing a real object with an implicit `undefined` hides this failure instead of surfacing it as an error.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, make the mock `renameLeaderboard` fail loudly instead of returning `undefined`: if `board(id)` is falsy, `throw new Error('that leaderboard no longer exists')`; otherwise apply the updates and return the board object, so the return type is always a board (or a thrown error) — matching the live `call('rename_leaderboard', ...)` path.
violations.snippet: renameLeaderboard: (id, name, game_types, points_target) => { const b = board(id); if (b) { b.name = name; if (game_types?.length) b.game_types = game_types; if (points_target) b.points_target = points_target; } return b; },

violations.title: `attempt` decides to lock the session by regex-matching the error message text
violations.content: `attempt` catches everything with no discrimination and then infers auth failure from `/passcode/i.test(e.message)`. This couples control flow to server-side prose: the server also returns messages that merely mention the passcode without being auth failures, and any future rewording of `'wrong passcode'` (index.ts:126) silently breaks the lock behaviour, leaving the user with a stale session. Conversely, an unrelated error whose text happens to contain "passcode" logs the user out. The catch also reads `e.message` unguarded, so a non-`Error` throw sets the error element to `undefined` and skips the lock. Every other failure is written to the DOM and swallowed with no logging, so unexpected client bugs leave no trace in the console.
violations.fixPrompt: Make the auth failure explicit instead of text-matched: in `js/api.js`, attach a status/code to the thrown error (e.g. `const err = new Error(out.error || `Request failed (${res.status})`); err.status = res.status; throw err;`), then in `attempt` in `js/app.js` branch on `e.status === 401` rather than `/passcode/i.test(e.message)`. Also guard the message extraction (`e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`) and `console.error(e)` before swallowing so the stack reaches the console.

violations.title: `refresh` and `switchBoard` reduce every failure to `e.message`, dropping stack and type
violations.content: Both `refresh` (lines 135–136) and `switchBoard` (line 142) catch broadly and keep only `e.message` in the `error` state variable, with no `console.error(e)`. The stack trace, error type, and any `cause` chain set upstream are discarded, so a `TypeError` inside `loadBoards`/`loadBoard` is indistinguishable from a server-reported validation failure and leaves nothing in the console to locate it. Because `e.message` is read unguarded, a non-`Error` throw (e.g. a rejected promise with a string) sets `error = undefined`, which renders as no error at all while the UI shows stale data.
violations.fixPrompt: In `refresh` and `switchBoard` in `js/app.js`, log the raw error before reducing it for display: `catch (e) { console.error(e); error = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e); }` so the stack survives in the console and non-`Error` throws still produce a visible message.
violations.snippet:
try { await loadBoards(); await loadBoard(); error = null; }
  catch (e) { error = e.message; }

violations.title: Module-level `data` and `boardId` overwritten by out-of-order `loadBoard` responses
violations.content:
`loadBoard` (line 132) reads the module-level `boardId` and writes the module-level `data` after an `await`, with no guard that `boardId` is still the board the fetch was started for. `switchBoard` sets `boardId` (line 140) and then awaits `loadBoard()`.

If a user switches boards twice in quick succession, both fetches are in flight; whichever resolves last wins. When the first (older board) response arrives second, `data` is set to the old board's payload while `boardId` and the persisted `LAST_BOARD` point at the new board, and `render()` then draws the wrong board's standings under the new board's header. `refresh()` (lines 134-138) has the same exposure — it is invoked from many click handlers (lines 204, 226, 242, 276, 286, 732, 809, 818, 824) that can overlap — and `loadBoards()` additionally reassigns `boardId` from a stale `boards` list.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, guard against out-of-order responses: keep a module-level request token (e.g. `let loadSeq = 0;`), capture `const seq = ++loadSeq;` and `const id = boardId;` at the start of `loadBoard`, and only assign `data = ...` if `seq === loadSeq && id === boardId` when the await resolves. Apply the same token check in `refresh` around the `loadBoards()`/`loadBoard()` pair so a stale refresh cannot clobber newer state.

violations.title: `playLoserSound` never disconnects its Web Audio nodes from the shared context
violations.content: `playLoserSound` creates a `BiquadFilter` (`lp`), an LFO oscillator plus `lfoGain`, and one `OscillatorNode`/`GainNode` pair per note, then connects `lp` to `ctx.destination`. `ctx` is the module-level `audioCtx` created once by `ensureAudio`, so it outlives every call. No node is ever `disconnect()`ed. The source oscillators are stopped and become collectible, but `lp` and `lfoGain` remain wired into the graph (`lp.connect(ctx.destination)` at line 868, `lfoGain.connect(osc.frequency)` at line 883), so each invocation grows the audio graph hanging off the shared destination. Over a long session with many logged games this accumulates filter/gain nodes that are never torn down.
violations.fixPrompt: In `playLoserSound` in `js/app.js`, tear down the audio graph once playback finishes. Track the last note's end time, and on the final oscillator attach an `onended` (or `addEventListener('ended', ...)`) handler that calls `disconnect()` on `lp`, `lfo`, `lfoGain`, and each per-note `osc`/`g` pair. Keep the existing `try`/`catch` so a missing-audio environment still degrades silently.

violations.title: `showPecundang` drops the previous toast without clearing its pending `setTimeout`
violations.content: `showPecundang` removes any existing toast with `document.querySelector('.pecundang')?.remove()` at line 897, but that bypasses the previous invocation's `close`, so the earlier `timer = setTimeout(close, 4200)` (line 910) is never cleared. The stale timer keeps the old closure — and through it the detached toast element and its `onUndo` callback — alive until it fires, at which point it calls `o.remove()` on an already-detached node. Only the `clearTimeout` inside `close` cleans this up, and that path is skipped when the toast is replaced rather than closed. Two games logged within 4.2 seconds of each other reproduce it.
violations.fixPrompt: In `showPecundang` in `js/app.js`, keep the pending timeout id in a module-level variable (e.g. `pecundangTimer`) instead of a purely local one. At the top of the function, call `clearTimeout(pecundangTimer)` alongside the existing `document.querySelector('.pecundang')?.remove()` so replacing a toast also cancels the previous timer, and have `close` clear that same variable.

violations.title: `log_sports_game` discards the `points_target` query error and silently falls back to 21
violations.content: Unlike every other query in this handler, the padel board lookup destructures only `data` and drops `error`. If the `leaderboards` select fails (connection error, RLS, timeout), `board` is `undefined` and `padelTarget` silently becomes `21`. Execution then continues as if the lookup succeeded: `scoreError(sport, score_a, score_b, 21)` validates the round against the wrong target and the game is inserted with `points_target: 21`, permanently snapshotting a value the board never configured. A board with `points_target: 32` would have rounds silently accepted/rejected against 21 and stored wrong, with no error surfaced to the caller and nothing logged.
violations.fixPrompt: In the `log_sports_game` case of `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, capture the error from the padel `points_target` lookup: `const { data: board, error: ebt } = await db.from('leaderboards').select('points_target').eq('id', leaderboard_id).maybeSingle();` then `if (ebt) return bad(ebt.message);` before defaulting `padelTarget = board?.points_target ?? 21`. Only fall back to 21 when the query succeeded and the column is null.
violations.snippet:
const { data: board } = await db.from('leaderboards').select('points_target').eq('id', leaderboard_id).maybeSingle();
          padelTarget = board?.points_target ?? 21;

violations.title: Top-level catch turns every unexpected failure into a 400 with a raw internal message
violations.content: The single `catch (e)` around the whole action switch performs no type discrimination and returns `bad(...)`, which defaults to HTTP 400. A `TypeError` from a null dereference, a Supabase client connection failure, or any other server-side fault is therefore reported to the client as a client-side validation error, sitting alongside genuine 400s like `'game_date must be YYYY-MM-DD'`. The client in `js/api.js` surfaces that raw message verbatim, so users see internal messages (and callers/monitoring cannot distinguish "your input was wrong" from "the server broke"). The blind `(e as Error)` cast also yields `undefined` for non-`Error` throws, producing `{"ok":false,"error":undefined}`.
violations.fixPrompt: In the top-level catch of `Deno.serve` in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, return a 500 with a generic client-facing message for unexpected errors (e.g. `return bad('internal error', 500)`), while logging the full detail server-side. Extract the message safely, e.g. `const msg = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e);`, instead of casting with `(e as Error)`.

violations.title: Top-level error log records only `message`, discarding the stack trace
violations.content: `log(false, { error: (e as Error).message })` is the only record of an unexpected server failure, and it keeps just the message. The stack trace, error name/type, and any `cause` chain are dropped, so a production failure logs something like `{"error":"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')"}` with no indication of which of the ~20 action branches threw it. That makes the most severe class of bug in this function the hardest one to diagnose.
violations.fixPrompt: In the top-level catch of `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, include the stack and type in the log payload, e.g. `log(false, { error: e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e), name: (e as Error)?.name, stack: (e as Error)?.stack })`, so the server log retains the full context.
violations.snippet: log(false, { error: (e as Error).message });

violations.title: `restore_player`'s 404 `'player not found'` branch is unreachable; PostgREST error is returned instead
violations.content: `.single()` makes PostgREST return an error (PGRST116, "JSON object requested, multiple (or no) rows returned") when the update matches zero rows, so `if (error) return bad(error.message)` fires first and `if (!data) return bad('player not found', 404)` is dead code. A request for a non-existent `player_id` gets a 400 with an opaque PostgREST message instead of the intended 404 `'player not found'`. `rename_leaderboard` at lines 160–162 has the identical dead 404 branch for `'leaderboard not found'`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `restore_player` (and `rename_leaderboard`) in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, use `.maybeSingle()` instead of `.single()` so a zero-row update yields `data === null` rather than an error, letting the intended `bad('player not found', 404)` / `bad('leaderboard not found', 404)` branch run. Alternatively, detect the `PGRST116` code on the error and map it to the 404 message.

violations.title: `add_player` forwards any DB error as a 400, though the comment assumes only a unique violation
violations.content: The comment ("unique(leaderboard_id,name) violation lands here") documents one expected cause, but `if (error) return bad(error.message)` funnels every failure — FK violation on a bad `leaderboard_id`, connection loss, statement timeout, permission error — through the same 400 response carrying a raw Postgres string. The user sees a duplicate-name style failure for what may be an infrastructure outage, and there is no `log(false, ...)` call on this path, so the failure is invisible in the logs too. The same undiscriminated `return bad(error.message)` pattern repeats across the switch (lines 146, 170, 202, 207, 244, 259, 271, 279, 340, 355, 369, 377, 412).
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, add a helper that maps Supabase/PostgREST errors to responses by `error.code` — e.g. `23505` (unique violation) → 400 with a friendly "a player with that name already exists", `23503` (FK violation) → 400 "unknown leaderboard", everything else → 500 with a generic message plus a `log(false, { code: error.code, message: error.message, details: error.details })` server-side entry. Route the `if (error)` branches through that helper instead of `bad(error.message)`.
violations.snippet:
const { data, error } = await db.from('players').insert({ leaderboard_id, name }).select().single();
        if (error) return bad(error.message); // unique(leaderboard_id,name) violation lands here

violations.title: Request body parse error is caught bare and discarded entirely
violations.content: `try { body = await req.json(); } catch { return bad('bad request'); }` binds no error variable, so the `SyntaxError` (which states exactly where the JSON is malformed) is thrown away and never logged. The caller receives only `'bad request'`, and the server keeps no record at all, making malformed-client-payload reports impossible to investigate.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, change the body parse to `catch (e) { console.log(JSON.stringify({ at: 'admin', ip, ok: false, error: 'bad json', detail: e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e) })); return bad('request body must be valid JSON'); }` so the parse detail is retained server-side.
violations.snippet: try { body = await req.json(); } catch { return bad('bad request'); }

violations.title: Rate-limit counter `fails` read before two `await`s, then written — lost updates defeat lockout
violations.content:
The module-level `fails` map is the only brute-force protection on the admin passcode. The handler reads `const rec = fails.get(ip)` at line 115, then crosses two async boundaries (`await req.json()` at line 119 and `await passcodeMatches(passcode)` at line 122) before writing `fails.set(ip, { n, ... })` at line 124, where `n` is derived from the stale `rec` captured earlier.

Deno serves requests concurrently in a single isolate, so N simultaneous wrong-passcode requests from the same IP all observe the same `rec.n` and all write back the same `n = rec.n + 1`. The counter advances by one instead of N, so an attacker issuing parallel (rather than serial) guesses can make far more than `MAX_FAILS` attempts before `until` is ever set. The same interleaving lets a request that read `rec` before a successful login's `fails.delete(ip)` (line 128) re-insert a stale counter afterwards.

The check at line 116 (`rec.until > now`) is likewise a check-then-act: the lockout decision is made on a snapshot taken before the passcode comparison, so requests already in flight when the lock engages are not blocked.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `fails` counter update atomic with respect to the read. Re-read the record from `fails` immediately before mutating it (after the `await passcodeMatches(...)` call) instead of reusing the `rec` snapshot captured at line 115, e.g. `const cur = fails.get(ip); const n = (cur?.n ?? 0) + 1; fails.set(ip, { n, until: n >= MAX_FAILS ? Date.now() + LOCK_MS : 0 });`. Also re-check the lockout (`cur.until > Date.now()`) at that point so requests that were in flight when the lock engaged are rejected.

violations.title: `undo_last` selects the newest game then deletes it in a separate query
violations.content:
`undo_last` reads the newest game id with one query (lines 251-255) and deletes it with a second query (line 258). Two concurrent undo requests for the same `leaderboard_id` both read the same `last.id`, then both issue the delete. The first removes the row; the second deletes zero rows but still returns `ok(last)` and logs success, so the user is told two games were undone when only one was. Conversely, a `log_game` that commits between the select and the delete causes the undo to remove the second-newest game rather than the one the user just logged.

The undo button is reachable from the "pecundang" overlay (`js/app.js:393-395`) which can be double-tapped, making the concurrent path reachable in normal use.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make `undo_last` atomic: perform the delete and read the affected row in one statement, e.g. a Postgres RPC (`delete from games where id = (select id from games where leaderboard_id = $1 order by created_at desc, id desc limit 1) returning id`) called via `db.rpc(...)`. If keeping two queries, add `.select()` to the delete and return `ok(null)` when no row was actually removed so a duplicate undo does not report false success.

violations.title: `undo_last_sports` selects the newest racquet game then deletes it non-atomically
violations.content: Same check-then-act pattern as `undo_last`: the newest `sports_games` row is selected (lines 347-351) and deleted in a separate query (line 354). Concurrent undos both read the same `last.id`; the losing request deletes nothing yet returns `ok(last)` and logs success. A `log_sports_game` committing between the two queries makes the undo delete the wrong round — particularly damaging during an Americano session where rounds are logged in rapid succession from `js/app.js:720-733`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make `undo_last_sports` atomic by moving the select+delete into a single Postgres RPC with `delete ... where id = (select ... limit 1) returning id`, or at minimum add `.select()` to the delete and return `ok(null)` when zero rows were removed.

violations.title: `delete_player` counts games then archives-or-deletes in a later query
violations.content:
`delete_player` counts the player's appearances in `games` and `sports_games` (lines 192-197) and then, based on that snapshot, either archives (line 201) or hard-deletes (line 206). A `log_game` or `log_sports_game` request that commits between the count and the delete makes the count stale: the code takes the `deleted: true` branch and the `ON DELETE RESTRICT` FK fires, surfacing exactly the "ugly error" the inline comment says this logic exists to avoid. The response is then a raw Postgres constraint message rather than the intended archive behaviour.

Note the inverse ordering also matters: `log_game` validates `archived` at line 240 and inserts at line 242, so a concurrent archive can still land a game on an archived player.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, move the archive-vs-delete decision for `delete_player` into a single Postgres function (called via `db.rpc`) that locks the player row (`select ... for update`), re-counts references, and archives or deletes within one transaction. As a minimum mitigation, catch a foreign-key violation from the delete at line 206 and fall back to setting `archived: true`, returning `{ archived: true, deleted: false }`.

violations.title: `undo_last` returns `data: null` on one branch and a game object on the other
violations.content: The `undo_last` case resolves its success payload to two different shapes: when there is no game to undo it returns `ok(null)` (line 257), giving the caller `{ ok: true, data: null }`; on the normal path it returns `ok(last)` (line 261), giving `{ ok: true, data: { id: number } }`. Both are `ok: true` responses, so a client that treats a successful response as "a game was deleted" and reads `data.id` will throw on an empty board. The no-op case is also indistinguishable from a real deletion without an extra null check, which the sibling `delete_game` / `delete_sports_game` handlers never require because they always return an object. A consistent contract — e.g. always returning `{ game_id: last?.id ?? null, deleted: !!last }` — would let callers use one code path.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `undo_last` case return a consistently shaped success payload. Replace `return ok(null)` (the `if (!last)` branch) and `return ok(last)` with a single object shape, e.g. `return ok({ game_id: null, deleted: false })` when there is nothing to undo and `return ok({ game_id: last.id, deleted: true })` after a successful delete. Update any front-end callers of the `undo_last` action that currently read `data` or `data.id` directly so they read the new fields.

violations.title: `undo_last_sports` returns `data: null` on one branch and a game object on the other
violations.content: Same inconsistency as `undo_last`: the `undo_last_sports` case returns `ok(null)` at line 353 when no sports game exists, and `ok(last)` (an object `{ id }`) at line 357 after deleting one. Both are `ok: true`, so callers cannot distinguish "nothing to undo" from "undo succeeded" without a null guard, and any code that reads `data.id` off a successful response will throw when the board has no logged rounds.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `undo_last_sports` case return one consistent success shape instead of mixing `null` and an object. Return e.g. `ok({ sports_game_id: null, deleted: false })` in the `if (!last)` branch and `ok({ sports_game_id: last.id, deleted: true })` after the delete succeeds, and update front-end callers of the `undo_last_sports` action accordingly.

violations.title: `call` swallows the JSON parse failure and reports a misleading `Request failed (200)`
violations.content: `res.json().catch(() => ({}))` discards the parse error and substitutes `{}`. For a successful HTTP response with an unparseable or empty body (proxy-truncated response, HTML error page from an edge failure, 204), `out.ok` is `undefined`, so line 213 throws `Request failed (200)` — an error message that contradicts itself and describes a failure mode that did not occur. The real cause (the body was not JSON) is completely lost, and the same message is produced for network-level and body-level problems alike.
violations.fixPrompt: In `call` in `js/api.js`, capture the parse failure distinctly, e.g. `let out; try { out = await res.json(); } catch (e) { throw new Error(res.ok ? `Server sent an unreadable response (${res.status})` : `Request failed (${res.status})`, { cause: e }); }` and only then check `!res.ok || !out.ok`.
violations.snippet:
const out = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
  if (!res.ok || !out.ok) throw new Error(out.error || `Request failed (${res.status})`);

violations.title: `loadBoard` uses `Promise.all`, so one failing query blanks the entire board
violations.content:
`loadBoard` fans out eight independent REST queries through `Promise.all`. `get` throws on any non-OK response (line 164), and `Promise.all` rejects on the first rejection, so a single failing or missing resource — for example the `padel_sessions` table or the `v_padel_standings` view returning 404/500 on a board that does not even play padel — discards the seven successful responses. The caller in `js/app.js:134-138` catches this and sets `error`, leaving the user with no standings, no games and no player list instead of a board that is merely missing its padel panel.

This is the failure mode where one unrelated query brings down every feature on the screen; the data is naturally partitionable and should degrade per-section.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, change `loadBoard` to use `Promise.allSettled` and map each result to its value or a safe empty fallback (`[]`), so a failure in one query does not discard the others. Keep hard-failing only for the queries the board cannot render without (e.g. `players` and `standings`), and return a per-section error marker for the rest so `js/app.js` can render a partial board with an inline notice instead of an empty screen.
violations.snippet:
const [standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions] = await Promise.all([
    get(`v_standings?select=player_id,name,gp,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_sport_standings?select=sport,player_id,name,games,losses,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&sport=neq.cards&order=name`),
    get(`v_padel_standings?select=player_id,name,archived,rounds,points_for,points_against&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`games?select=id,game_date,p1,p2,p3,p4,loser,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`sports_games?select=id,game_date,sport,a1,a2,b1,b2,score_a,score_b,points_target,session_id,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=game_date.desc,created_at.desc`),
    get(`players?select=id,name,archived&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=name`),
    get(`v_daily_losses?select=player_id,name,losses&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&game_date=eq.${today}`),
    get(`padel_sessions?select=id,game_date,roster,courts,rounds,created_at&leaderboard_id=eq.${id}&order=created_at.desc`),
  ]);
  return { standings, sportStandings, padelStandings, games, sportsGames, players, dailyLosses, padelSessions };

violations.title: `listLeaderboards` returns a raw array in mock mode but a Promise otherwise
violations.content: `listLeaderboards` is declared as a plain arrow function whose two branches return different kinds of value: when `USE_MOCK` is true it returns the synchronous array produced by `mock.listLeaderboards()`, and otherwise it returns the Promise returned by `get(...)`. The return type is therefore `Array | Promise<Array>` depending on a module-level flag. It happens to work today only because every caller (`loadBoards` in `js/app.js`) awaits the result, and `await` on a non-thenable is a no-op. Any caller that treats the result synchronously (or that chains `.then`/`.catch` on it) would break in exactly one of the two modes, and the mock branch silently swallows the possibility of rejection handling. The same shape is repeated in every exported wrapper in this file.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, make the mock and live branches return the same wrapped type. Either declare `listLeaderboards` as `async` (so the mock branch is auto-wrapped in a Promise), or wrap the mock branch explicitly with `Promise.resolve(...)`. Apply the same treatment to the other exported wrappers (`createLeaderboard`, `renameLeaderboard`, `deleteLeaderboard`, `addPlayer`, `deletePlayer`, `restorePlayer`, `logGame`, `undoLast`, `editLoser`, `deleteGame`, `logSportsGame`, `createPadelSession`, `undoLastSports`, `editSportsScore`, `deleteSportsGame`) so every export consistently returns a Promise.
violations.snippet:
export const listLeaderboards = () =>
  USE_MOCK ? mock.listLeaderboards() : get('leaderboards?select=id,name,game_types,points_target&order=name');

violations.title: `logSportsGame` returns either a plain object or a Promise depending on `USE_MOCK`
violations.content: `logSportsGame` explicitly returns the result of a ternary whose branches have different types: `mock.logSportsGame(...)` returns the newly created game object synchronously, while `call('log_sports_game', ...)` returns a Promise resolving to the server row. Callers such as the `save` handler in `openLogSport` and the round-runner's log handler in `js/app.js` pass this through `attempt(...)`, which awaits it — so failures in the mock branch would throw synchronously at call time rather than rejecting, and error handling differs between the two modes. A function that sometimes returns a wrapped value and sometimes the raw value is easy to misuse as the codebase grows.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, mark `logSportsGame` as `async` (or wrap the mock branch in `Promise.resolve(...)`) so both branches return a Promise resolving to the created sports-game row, regardless of `USE_MOCK`.

violations.title: Mock `renameLeaderboard` returns `undefined` when the board id is unknown
violations.content: `renameLeaderboard` in the mock backend does `const b = board(id); if (b) { ... } return b;` — so when `board(id)` finds no matching board it returns `undefined`, while the success path returns the mutated board object and the live path (`call('rename_leaderboard', ...)`) resolves to a server row. The caller in `openRenameBoard` (`js/app.js`) treats any non-throwing result as success, so a rename against a stale or deleted `boardId` in mock mode silently reports success and closes the sheet even though nothing was renamed. Mixing a real object with an implicit `undefined` hides this failure instead of surfacing it as an error.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/api.js`, make the mock `renameLeaderboard` fail loudly instead of returning `undefined`: if `board(id)` is falsy, `throw new Error('that leaderboard no longer exists')`; otherwise apply the updates and return the board object, so the return type is always a board (or a thrown error) — matching the live `call('rename_leaderboard', ...)` path.
violations.snippet: renameLeaderboard: (id, name, game_types, points_target) => { const b = board(id); if (b) { b.name = name; if (game_types?.length) b.game_types = game_types; if (points_target) b.points_target = points_target; } return b; },

violations.title: `attempt` decides to lock the session by regex-matching the error message text
violations.content: `attempt` catches everything with no discrimination and then infers auth failure from `/passcode/i.test(e.message)`. This couples control flow to server-side prose: the server also returns messages that merely mention the passcode without being auth failures, and any future rewording of `'wrong passcode'` (index.ts:126) silently breaks the lock behaviour, leaving the user with a stale session. Conversely, an unrelated error whose text happens to contain "passcode" logs the user out. The catch also reads `e.message` unguarded, so a non-`Error` throw sets the error element to `undefined` and skips the lock. Every other failure is written to the DOM and swallowed with no logging, so unexpected client bugs leave no trace in the console.
violations.fixPrompt: Make the auth failure explicit instead of text-matched: in `js/api.js`, attach a status/code to the thrown error (e.g. `const err = new Error(out.error || `Request failed (${res.status})`); err.status = res.status; throw err;`), then in `attempt` in `js/app.js` branch on `e.status === 401` rather than `/passcode/i.test(e.message)`. Also guard the message extraction (`e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`) and `console.error(e)` before swallowing so the stack reaches the console.

violations.title: `refresh` and `switchBoard` reduce every failure to `e.message`, dropping stack and type
violations.content: Both `refresh` (lines 135–136) and `switchBoard` (line 142) catch broadly and keep only `e.message` in the `error` state variable, with no `console.error(e)`. The stack trace, error type, and any `cause` chain set upstream are discarded, so a `TypeError` inside `loadBoards`/`loadBoard` is indistinguishable from a server-reported validation failure and leaves nothing in the console to locate it. Because `e.message` is read unguarded, a non-`Error` throw (e.g. a rejected promise with a string) sets `error = undefined`, which renders as no error at all while the UI shows stale data.
violations.fixPrompt: In `refresh` and `switchBoard` in `js/app.js`, log the raw error before reducing it for display: `catch (e) { console.error(e); error = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e); }` so the stack survives in the console and non-`Error` throws still produce a visible message.
violations.snippet:
try { await loadBoards(); await loadBoard(); error = null; }
  catch (e) { error = e.message; }

violations.title: Module-level `data` and `boardId` overwritten by out-of-order `loadBoard` responses
violations.content:
`loadBoard` (line 132) reads the module-level `boardId` and writes the module-level `data` after an `await`, with no guard that `boardId` is still the board the fetch was started for. `switchBoard` sets `boardId` (line 140) and then awaits `loadBoard()`.

If a user switches boards twice in quick succession, both fetches are in flight; whichever resolves last wins. When the first (older board) response arrives second, `data` is set to the old board's payload while `boardId` and the persisted `LAST_BOARD` point at the new board, and `render()` then draws the wrong board's standings under the new board's header. `refresh()` (lines 134-138) has the same exposure — it is invoked from many click handlers (lines 204, 226, 242, 276, 286, 732, 809, 818, 824) that can overlap — and `loadBoards()` additionally reassigns `boardId` from a stale `boards` list.
violations.fixPrompt: In `js/app.js`, guard against out-of-order responses: keep a module-level request token (e.g. `let loadSeq = 0;`), capture `const seq = ++loadSeq;` and `const id = boardId;` at the start of `loadBoard`, and only assign `data = ...` if `seq === loadSeq && id === boardId` when the await resolves. Apply the same token check in `refresh` around the `loadBoards()`/`loadBoard()` pair so a stale refresh cannot clobber newer state.

violations.title: `playLoserSound` never disconnects its Web Audio nodes from the shared context
violations.content: `playLoserSound` creates a `BiquadFilter` (`lp`), an LFO oscillator plus `lfoGain`, and one `OscillatorNode`/`GainNode` pair per note, then connects `lp` to `ctx.destination`. `ctx` is the module-level `audioCtx` created once by `ensureAudio`, so it outlives every call. No node is ever `disconnect()`ed. The source oscillators are stopped and become collectible, but `lp` and `lfoGain` remain wired into the graph (`lp.connect(ctx.destination)` at line 868, `lfoGain.connect(osc.frequency)` at line 883), so each invocation grows the audio graph hanging off the shared destination. Over a long session with many logged games this accumulates filter/gain nodes that are never torn down.
violations.fixPrompt: In `playLoserSound` in `js/app.js`, tear down the audio graph once playback finishes. Track the last note's end time, and on the final oscillator attach an `onended` (or `addEventListener('ended', ...)`) handler that calls `disconnect()` on `lp`, `lfo`, `lfoGain`, and each per-note `osc`/`g` pair. Keep the existing `try`/`catch` so a missing-audio environment still degrades silently.

violations.title: `showPecundang` drops the previous toast without clearing its pending `setTimeout`
violations.content: `showPecundang` removes any existing toast with `document.querySelector('.pecundang')?.remove()` at line 897, but that bypasses the previous invocation's `close`, so the earlier `timer = setTimeout(close, 4200)` (line 910) is never cleared. The stale timer keeps the old closure — and through it the detached toast element and its `onUndo` callback — alive until it fires, at which point it calls `o.remove()` on an already-detached node. Only the `clearTimeout` inside `close` cleans this up, and that path is skipped when the toast is replaced rather than closed. Two games logged within 4.2 seconds of each other reproduce it.
violations.fixPrompt: In `showPecundang` in `js/app.js`, keep the pending timeout id in a module-level variable (e.g. `pecundangTimer`) instead of a purely local one. At the top of the function, call `clearTimeout(pecundangTimer)` alongside the existing `document.querySelector('.pecundang')?.remove()` so replacing a toast also cancels the previous timer, and have `close` clear that same variable.

violations.title: `log_sports_game` discards the `points_target` query error and silently falls back to 21
violations.content: Unlike every other query in this handler, the padel board lookup destructures only `data` and drops `error`. If the `leaderboards` select fails (connection error, RLS, timeout), `board` is `undefined` and `padelTarget` silently becomes `21`. Execution then continues as if the lookup succeeded: `scoreError(sport, score_a, score_b, 21)` validates the round against the wrong target and the game is inserted with `points_target: 21`, permanently snapshotting a value the board never configured. A board with `points_target: 32` would have rounds silently accepted/rejected against 21 and stored wrong, with no error surfaced to the caller and nothing logged.
violations.fixPrompt: In the `log_sports_game` case of `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, capture the error from the padel `points_target` lookup: `const { data: board, error: ebt } = await db.from('leaderboards').select('points_target').eq('id', leaderboard_id).maybeSingle();` then `if (ebt) return bad(ebt.message);` before defaulting `padelTarget = board?.points_target ?? 21`. Only fall back to 21 when the query succeeded and the column is null.
violations.snippet:
const { data: board } = await db.from('leaderboards').select('points_target').eq('id', leaderboard_id).maybeSingle();
          padelTarget = board?.points_target ?? 21;

violations.title: Top-level catch turns every unexpected failure into a 400 with a raw internal message
violations.content: The single `catch (e)` around the whole action switch performs no type discrimination and returns `bad(...)`, which defaults to HTTP 400. A `TypeError` from a null dereference, a Supabase client connection failure, or any other server-side fault is therefore reported to the client as a client-side validation error, sitting alongside genuine 400s like `'game_date must be YYYY-MM-DD'`. The client in `js/api.js` surfaces that raw message verbatim, so users see internal messages (and callers/monitoring cannot distinguish "your input was wrong" from "the server broke"). The blind `(e as Error)` cast also yields `undefined` for non-`Error` throws, producing `{"ok":false,"error":undefined}`.
violations.fixPrompt: In the top-level catch of `Deno.serve` in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, return a 500 with a generic client-facing message for unexpected errors (e.g. `return bad('internal error', 500)`), while logging the full detail server-side. Extract the message safely, e.g. `const msg = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e);`, instead of casting with `(e as Error)`.

violations.title: Top-level error log records only `message`, discarding the stack trace
violations.content: `log(false, { error: (e as Error).message })` is the only record of an unexpected server failure, and it keeps just the message. The stack trace, error name/type, and any `cause` chain are dropped, so a production failure logs something like `{"error":"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')"}` with no indication of which of the ~20 action branches threw it. That makes the most severe class of bug in this function the hardest one to diagnose.
violations.fixPrompt: In the top-level catch of `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, include the stack and type in the log payload, e.g. `log(false, { error: e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e), name: (e as Error)?.name, stack: (e as Error)?.stack })`, so the server log retains the full context.
violations.snippet: log(false, { error: (e as Error).message });

violations.title: `restore_player`'s 404 `'player not found'` branch is unreachable; PostgREST error is returned instead
violations.content: `.single()` makes PostgREST return an error (PGRST116, "JSON object requested, multiple (or no) rows returned") when the update matches zero rows, so `if (error) return bad(error.message)` fires first and `if (!data) return bad('player not found', 404)` is dead code. A request for a non-existent `player_id` gets a 400 with an opaque PostgREST message instead of the intended 404 `'player not found'`. `rename_leaderboard` at lines 160–162 has the identical dead 404 branch for `'leaderboard not found'`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `restore_player` (and `rename_leaderboard`) in `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, use `.maybeSingle()` instead of `.single()` so a zero-row update yields `data === null` rather than an error, letting the intended `bad('player not found', 404)` / `bad('leaderboard not found', 404)` branch run. Alternatively, detect the `PGRST116` code on the error and map it to the 404 message.

violations.title: `add_player` forwards any DB error as a 400, though the comment assumes only a unique violation
violations.content: The comment ("unique(leaderboard_id,name) violation lands here") documents one expected cause, but `if (error) return bad(error.message)` funnels every failure — FK violation on a bad `leaderboard_id`, connection loss, statement timeout, permission error — through the same 400 response carrying a raw Postgres string. The user sees a duplicate-name style failure for what may be an infrastructure outage, and there is no `log(false, ...)` call on this path, so the failure is invisible in the logs too. The same undiscriminated `return bad(error.message)` pattern repeats across the switch (lines 146, 170, 202, 207, 244, 259, 271, 279, 340, 355, 369, 377, 412).
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, add a helper that maps Supabase/PostgREST errors to responses by `error.code` — e.g. `23505` (unique violation) → 400 with a friendly "a player with that name already exists", `23503` (FK violation) → 400 "unknown leaderboard", everything else → 500 with a generic message plus a `log(false, { code: error.code, message: error.message, details: error.details })` server-side entry. Route the `if (error)` branches through that helper instead of `bad(error.message)`.
violations.snippet:
const { data, error } = await db.from('players').insert({ leaderboard_id, name }).select().single();
        if (error) return bad(error.message); // unique(leaderboard_id,name) violation lands here

violations.title: Request body parse error is caught bare and discarded entirely
violations.content: `try { body = await req.json(); } catch { return bad('bad request'); }` binds no error variable, so the `SyntaxError` (which states exactly where the JSON is malformed) is thrown away and never logged. The caller receives only `'bad request'`, and the server keeps no record at all, making malformed-client-payload reports impossible to investigate.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, change the body parse to `catch (e) { console.log(JSON.stringify({ at: 'admin', ip, ok: false, error: 'bad json', detail: e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e) })); return bad('request body must be valid JSON'); }` so the parse detail is retained server-side.
violations.snippet: try { body = await req.json(); } catch { return bad('bad request'); }

violations.title: Rate-limit counter `fails` read before two `await`s, then written — lost updates defeat lockout
violations.content:
The module-level `fails` map is the only brute-force protection on the admin passcode. The handler reads `const rec = fails.get(ip)` at line 115, then crosses two async boundaries (`await req.json()` at line 119 and `await passcodeMatches(passcode)` at line 122) before writing `fails.set(ip, { n, ... })` at line 124, where `n` is derived from the stale `rec` captured earlier.

Deno serves requests concurrently in a single isolate, so N simultaneous wrong-passcode requests from the same IP all observe the same `rec.n` and all write back the same `n = rec.n + 1`. The counter advances by one instead of N, so an attacker issuing parallel (rather than serial) guesses can make far more than `MAX_FAILS` attempts before `until` is ever set. The same interleaving lets a request that read `rec` before a successful login's `fails.delete(ip)` (line 128) re-insert a stale counter afterwards.

The check at line 116 (`rec.until > now`) is likewise a check-then-act: the lockout decision is made on a snapshot taken before the passcode comparison, so requests already in flight when the lock engages are not blocked.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `fails` counter update atomic with respect to the read. Re-read the record from `fails` immediately before mutating it (after the `await passcodeMatches(...)` call) instead of reusing the `rec` snapshot captured at line 115, e.g. `const cur = fails.get(ip); const n = (cur?.n ?? 0) + 1; fails.set(ip, { n, until: n >= MAX_FAILS ? Date.now() + LOCK_MS : 0 });`. Also re-check the lockout (`cur.until > Date.now()`) at that point so requests that were in flight when the lock engaged are rejected.

violations.title: `undo_last` selects the newest game then deletes it in a separate query
violations.content:
`undo_last` reads the newest game id with one query (lines 251-255) and deletes it with a second query (line 258). Two concurrent undo requests for the same `leaderboard_id` both read the same `last.id`, then both issue the delete. The first removes the row; the second deletes zero rows but still returns `ok(last)` and logs success, so the user is told two games were undone when only one was. Conversely, a `log_game` that commits between the select and the delete causes the undo to remove the second-newest game rather than the one the user just logged.

The undo button is reachable from the "pecundang" overlay (`js/app.js:393-395`) which can be double-tapped, making the concurrent path reachable in normal use.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make `undo_last` atomic: perform the delete and read the affected row in one statement, e.g. a Postgres RPC (`delete from games where id = (select id from games where leaderboard_id = $1 order by created_at desc, id desc limit 1) returning id`) called via `db.rpc(...)`. If keeping two queries, add `.select()` to the delete and return `ok(null)` when no row was actually removed so a duplicate undo does not report false success.

violations.title: `undo_last_sports` selects the newest racquet game then deletes it non-atomically
violations.content: Same check-then-act pattern as `undo_last`: the newest `sports_games` row is selected (lines 347-351) and deleted in a separate query (line 354). Concurrent undos both read the same `last.id`; the losing request deletes nothing yet returns `ok(last)` and logs success. A `log_sports_game` committing between the two queries makes the undo delete the wrong round — particularly damaging during an Americano session where rounds are logged in rapid succession from `js/app.js:720-733`.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make `undo_last_sports` atomic by moving the select+delete into a single Postgres RPC with `delete ... where id = (select ... limit 1) returning id`, or at minimum add `.select()` to the delete and return `ok(null)` when zero rows were removed.

violations.title: `delete_player` counts games then archives-or-deletes in a later query
violations.content:
`delete_player` counts the player's appearances in `games` and `sports_games` (lines 192-197) and then, based on that snapshot, either archives (line 201) or hard-deletes (line 206). A `log_game` or `log_sports_game` request that commits between the count and the delete makes the count stale: the code takes the `deleted: true` branch and the `ON DELETE RESTRICT` FK fires, surfacing exactly the "ugly error" the inline comment says this logic exists to avoid. The response is then a raw Postgres constraint message rather than the intended archive behaviour.

Note the inverse ordering also matters: `log_game` validates `archived` at line 240 and inserts at line 242, so a concurrent archive can still land a game on an archived player.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, move the archive-vs-delete decision for `delete_player` into a single Postgres function (called via `db.rpc`) that locks the player row (`select ... for update`), re-counts references, and archives or deletes within one transaction. As a minimum mitigation, catch a foreign-key violation from the delete at line 206 and fall back to setting `archived: true`, returning `{ archived: true, deleted: false }`.

violations.title: `undo_last` returns `data: null` on one branch and a game object on the other
violations.content: The `undo_last` case resolves its success payload to two different shapes: when there is no game to undo it returns `ok(null)` (line 257), giving the caller `{ ok: true, data: null }`; on the normal path it returns `ok(last)` (line 261), giving `{ ok: true, data: { id: number } }`. Both are `ok: true` responses, so a client that treats a successful response as "a game was deleted" and reads `data.id` will throw on an empty board. The no-op case is also indistinguishable from a real deletion without an extra null check, which the sibling `delete_game` / `delete_sports_game` handlers never require because they always return an object. A consistent contract — e.g. always returning `{ game_id: last?.id ?? null, deleted: !!last }` — would let callers use one code path.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `undo_last` case return a consistently shaped success payload. Replace `return ok(null)` (the `if (!last)` branch) and `return ok(last)` with a single object shape, e.g. `return ok({ game_id: null, deleted: false })` when there is nothing to undo and `return ok({ game_id: last.id, deleted: true })` after a successful delete. Update any front-end callers of the `undo_last` action that currently read `data` or `data.id` directly so they read the new fields.

violations.title: `undo_last_sports` returns `data: null` on one branch and a game object on the other
violations.content: Same inconsistency as `undo_last`: the `undo_last_sports` case returns `ok(null)` at line 353 when no sports game exists, and `ok(last)` (an object `{ id }`) at line 357 after deleting one. Both are `ok: true`, so callers cannot distinguish "nothing to undo" from "undo succeeded" without a null guard, and any code that reads `data.id` off a successful response will throw when the board has no logged rounds.
violations.fixPrompt: In `supabase/functions/admin/index.ts`, make the `undo_last_sports` case return one consistent success shape instead of mixing `null` and an object. Return e.g. `ok({ sports_game_id: null, deleted: false })` in the `if (!last)` branch and `ok({ sports_game_id: last.id, deleted: true })` after the delete succeeds, and update front-end callers of the `undo_last_sports` action accordingly.

violations.title: `attempt` decides to lock the session by regex-matching the error message text
violations.content: `attempt` catches everything with no discrimination and then infers auth failure from `/passcode/i.test(e.message)`. This couples control flow to server-side prose: the server also returns messages that merely mention the passcode without being auth failures, and any future rewording of `'wrong passcode'` (index.ts:126) silently breaks the lock behaviour, leaving the user with a stale session. Conversely, an unrelated error whose text happens to contain "passcode" logs the user out. The catch also reads `e.message` unguarded, so a non-`Error` throw sets the error element to `undefined` and skips the lock. Every other failure is written to the DOM and swallowed with no logging, so unexpected client bugs leave no trace in the console.
violations.fixPrompt: Make the auth failure explicit instead of text-matched: in `js/api.js`, attach a status/code to the thrown error (e.g. `const err = new Error(out.error || `Request failed (${res.status})`); err.status = res.status; throw err;`), then in `attempt` in `js/app.js` branch on `e.status === 401` rather than `/passcode/i.test(e.message)`. Also guard the message extraction (`e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`) and `console.error(e)` before swallowing so the stack reaches the console.

violations.title: `refresh` and `switchBoard` reduce every failure to `e.message`, dropping stack and type
violations.content: Both `refresh` (lines 135–136) and `switchBoard` (line 142) catch broadly and keep only `e.message` in the `error` state variable, with no `console.error(e)`. The stack trace, error type, and any `cause` chain set upstream are discarded, so a `TypeError` inside `loadBoards`/`loadBoard` is indistinguishable from a server-reported validation failure and leaves nothing in the console to locate it. Because `e.message` is read unguarded, a non-`Error` throw (e.g. a rejected promise with a string) sets `error = undefined`, which renders as no error at all while the UI shows stale data.
violations.fixPrompt: In `refresh` and `switchBoard` in `js/app.js`, log the raw error before reducing it for display: `catch (e) { console.error(e); error = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e); }` so the stack survives in the console and non-`Error` throws still produce a visible message.
violations.snippet:
try { await loadBoards(); await loadBoard(); error = null; }
  catch (e) { error = e.message; }
